'''Theodore Crawford Cassidy''' (July 31, 1932 – January 16, 1979) was an American actor. He tended to play unusual characters in offbeat or science-fiction works, such as ''[[Star Trek: The Original Series|Star Trek]]'' and ''[[I Dream of Jeannie]]'', and he played [[Lurch (The Addams Family)|Lurch]] on ''[[The Addams Family (1964 TV series)|The Addams Family]]'' TV series of the mid-1960s.<ref name=NYT/><ref name= fsgymtotv>{{cite news |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=M9IhAAAAIBAJ&pg=4066%2C892148 |newspaper= [[Daytona Beach Morning Journal]] |location= Florida |title= From Stetson gym to TV stage |date= October 4, 1964 |page= 12, All Florida |access-date= }}</ref> He also narrated the intro sequence for the 1977 live-action [[The Incredible Hulk (1978 TV series)|''The Incredible Hulk'']] TV series and provided the growls and roars for the [[Hulk]] for the first two seasons before his death, with actor [[Charles Napier (actor)|Charles Napier]] providing the title character's vocals for the remainder of the series.<ref name="NYT">{{cite web |title= Ted Cassidy |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160121223701/http://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/11663/Ted-Cassidy/biography |archive-date= January 21, 2016 |url-status= dead |department= Movies & TV Dept. |work= [[The New York Times]] |first= Hal |last= Erickson |author-link= Hal Erickson (author) |year= 2016 |url= https://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/11663/Ted-Cassidy/biography |access-date= }}</ref><ref name=NYT2>{{cite web |work= The New York Times |url= https://www.nytimes.com/1979/01/24/archives/ted-cassidy-lurch-in-tv-series.html |title= Ted Cassidy, Lurch in TV Series |date= January 24, 1979 |archive-date= May 11, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180511013428/https://www.nytimes.com/1979/01/24/archives/ted-cassidy-lurch-in-tv-series.html |url-status= live |access-date= May 10, 2018}}</ref>

==Early life, family and education==
Cassidy was born in [[Pittsburgh]], [[Pennsylvania]], to Elwood Lewis Cassidy and Emily Cassidy (nee Crawford), who were of Irish ancestry. He was raised, however, in [[Philippi, West Virginia]],<ref>{{cite news |title= 'Lurch' Will Crown Strawberry Queen |url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-charleston-daily-mail-ted-cassidy-1/170837154/ |work= [[The Charleston Daily Mail]] |date= April 19, 1966 |location= Charleston, West Virginia |page= 8 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] |access-date= April 22, 2025}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title= Cass Special to Huff, Puff at 25th Strawberry Festival |url= https://www.newspapers.com/article/sunday-gazette-mail-ted-cassidy-1932-19/170836992/ |work= Sunday Gazette-Mail |date= June 5, 1966 |location= Charleston, West Virginia |page= 36 |via= [[Newspapers.com]] |access-date= April 22, 2025}} {{Open access}}</ref> where his father was an agent for the [[Eaton, Crane & Pike Company Factory|Eaton Paper Company]]. He was academically gifted and attended third grade at age six.<ref name="NYT"/> During his freshman year of high school, at age 11, he was on the [[High school football|football]] and [[High school basketball|basketball]] teams.<ref name="biocom">{{cite web |title= Ted Cassidy Biography – Television Actor (1932–1979) |url= http://www.biography.com/people/ted-cassidy-248965#awesm=~oIomAhUEu1h6pk |url-status= live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140808065224/http://www.biography.com/people/ted-cassidy-248965#awesm=~oIomAhUEu1h6pk |archive-date= August 8, 2014 |work= biography.com |access-date= June 27, 2014}}</ref>

After graduating from high school, Cassidy attended [[West Virginia Wesleyan College]] in [[Buckhannon, West Virginia|Buckhannon]] (1948–50), where he was a member of the [[Alpha Sigma Phi]] [[College fraternities and sororities|fraternity]]. He transferred to [[Stetson University]] in [[DeLand, Florida]],<ref name=volusn>{{cite news |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=yowfAAAAIBAJ&pg=1871%2C3113787 |newspaper= [[The Volusian]] |location= Florida |last= Plaisted |first= Ed |title= Ex-coach remembers Stetson days when 'Lurch' played basketball |date= March 22, 1995 |page= 1B |archive-date= September 28, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200928133637/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=yowfAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ftMEAAAAIBAJ&pg=1871%2C3113787 |url-status= live |access-date= May 13, 2016}}</ref> where he played [[college basketball]] for the [[Stetson Hatters men's basketball|Hatters]] (1954–55) and was active in the [[student government]].<ref>{{cite web |title= Stetson University |url= http://archives.stetson.edu:8888/cdm4/document.php?CISOROOT=%2Fyearbook&CISOPTR=8420&REC=2&CISOBOX=Cassidy |archive-url= https://archive.today/20130409234945/http://archives.stetson.edu:8888/cdm4/document.php?CISOROOT=/yearbook&CISOPTR=8420&REC=2&CISOBOX=Cassidy |url-status= dead |archive-date= April 9, 2013 |work= 1955 Hatter |via= archives.stetson.edu |format= Yearbook |access-date= }}</ref> He graduated from Stetson University with a BA degree. 

==Career==
[[File:WCOA Pensacola January 1959 20230917 0004 small.jpg|thumb|Ted Cassidy on air at WCOA Pensacola January 1959]]
Cassidy began his broadcast career at [[WCOA (AM)|WCOA]] in [[Pensacola, Florida]], during the summer of 1958 and through the fall of 1959. He relocated to [[Dallas]], [[Texas]], to work as a DJ on [[WFAA]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web |url= https://www.cbsnews.com/texas/news/the-foote-files-remembering-ted-cassidy/ |title= The Foote Files: Remembering Ted Cassidy |date= May 19, 2017 |publisher= CBS Texas |website= cbsnews.com| access-date= 2023-05-28}}</ref> He was an accomplished musician and [[wikt:moonlighting|moonlighted]], playing an [[organ (music)|organ]] at a [[Luby's]] Cafeteria in Dallas' Lochwood Shopping Center.<ref>{{cite web |title= Lurch (aka Ted Cassidy) |url= http://phorum.dallashistory.org/read.php?2,69188,69200 |website= phorum.dallashistory.org |year= 2010 |access-date= 24 May 2023}}</ref> He "was right in the middle of the excitement" on the day [[Assassination of John F. Kennedy|John F. Kennedy was assassinated]]<ref name=btkfsmh>{{cite news |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ZJYuAAAAIBAJ&pg=7027%2C2047793 |newspaper= [[The Bryan Times]] |location= Bryan, Ohio |agency= King Features Syndicate |last= Heimer |first= Mel |title= 'Lurch' moves on, 'Injun Joe' soon |date= August 16, 1967 |page= 5 |archive-date= September 28, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200928133719/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ZJYuAAAAIBAJ&sjid=IUgDAAAAIBAJ&pg=7027%2C2047793 |url-status= live |access-date= May 13, 2016}}</ref> and was among the first to interview eyewitnesses W. E. Newman Jr. and Gayle Newman.<ref>{{cite video |title= JFK's Assassination (11/22/63) (WFAA-Radio; Dallas) |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8J7H1gdg8Ug |via= YouTube |at= 0:43:05 |access-date= }}</ref>

===Television===
[[File:Fester lurch 1966.JPG|thumb|right|Cassidy (right) in'' The Addams Family ''with [[Jackie Coogan]] in 1966]]
Cassidy's height gave him an advantage in auditioning for unusual character roles.<ref name="biocom" /> His best-known role is Lurch on ''[[The Addams Family (1964 TV series)|The Addams Family]]'', in which he feigned playing the [[harpsichord]] (although he was in fact an accomplished organist).<ref>According to the ''Addams Family, Season 1, Volume 1'' DVD of the original TV series, music composer [[Vic Mizzy]] states that Lurch is playing on a dead keyboard, and though Cassidy was an accomplished organist, Mizzy played all the parts. This is shown in the Snap Snap special feature.</ref> With a separate contract, he also played the character named [[Thing (The Addams Family)|Thing]],<ref name="sauer20191011">{{cite magazine |last= Sauer |first= Patrick J. |date= 2019-10-11 |title= The Cultural History of 'The Addams Family' |url= https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/cultural-history-addams-family-180973315/ |magazine= [[Smithsonian (magazine)|Smithsonian]] |access-date= 2024-09-28}}</ref> though associate producer Jack Voglin took on the role in scenes involving both characters. Though the character of Lurch was originally intended to be mute, Cassidy's ad-libbed "You rang?" in response to the butler call was an immediate hit. It became his signature line, and he was given more lines. Several episodes were written to feature Lurch.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.legacy.com/news/legends-and-legacies/ted-cassidy-you-rang/1886/ |title= Ted Cassidy, You Rang? |work= Legacy.com |date= January 16, 2014 |archive-date= September 4, 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150904043731/http://www.legacy.com/news/legends-and-legacies/ted-cassidy-you-rang/1886/ |url-status= live |access-date= August 24, 2015}}</ref>

Cassidy reprised the role of Lurch in later appearances. In the ''[[Batman (TV series)|Batman]]'' episode "The Penguin's Nest" (1966), he appears during the heroes' familiar climbing scene up the side of a building, as a tenant who is playing the ''Addams Family'' theme on a harpsichord prior to sticking his head out of the window and speaking to Batman and Robin. He voiced Lurch in an episode of ''[[The New Scooby-Doo Movies]]'' (1972), and in the [[The Addams Family (1973 TV series)|1973 animated series]] adaptation of ''The Addams Family''. He again reprised Lurch in the TV film'' [[Halloween with the New Addams Family]]'' (1977).

According to Thomas "Duke" Miller, a TV/movie/celebrity expert, Cassidy also had a small role opposite [[George Peppard]] in one episode of the TV movie series ''[[Banacek]]''. Cassidy played a worker in an auto scrapyard who attempted to kill Banacek because the investigator traced him as part of the plot to steal a rare and valuable book.{{citation needed |date= November 2024}} In addition to ''The Addams Family'', Cassidy found steady work in a variety of other television shows.<ref name=btkfsmh /> He had a prominent role on [[NBC]]'s ''[[The New Adventures of Huckleberry Finn]]'' as [[Injun Joe]], the enemy of [[Tom Sawyer]] and [[Huckleberry Finn]].<ref>{{cite book |last= Erickson |first= Hal |title= Television Cartoon Shows: An Illustrated Encyclopedia, 1949 Through 2003 |year= 2005 |edition= 2nd |publisher= McFarland & Co |isbn= 978-1476665993 |pages= 584–586}}</ref> In the 1967 ''[[The Man from U.N.C.L.E.]]'' episode "The Napoleon's Tomb Affair", Cassidy played a henchman, Edgar, who kidnaps, tortures, and repeatedly tries to kill Napoleon and Illya.

Cassidy also provided the voices of the more aggressive version of Balok in the ''[[Star Trek: The Original Series|Star Trek]]'' episode "[[The Corbomite Maneuver]]" and the [[Gorn]] in the episode "[[Arena (Star Trek: The Original Series)|Arena]]", and played the part of the [[Android (robot)|android]] Ruk in the episode "[[What Are Little Girls Made Of?]]". Cassidy did more work with ''Star Trek'' creator [[Gene Roddenberry]] in the early 1970s, playing Isaiah in the [[postapocalyptic]] drama pilots ''[[Genesis II (film)|Genesis II]]'' and ''[[Planet Earth (TV pilot)|Planet Earth]]''. In the ''[[Lost in Space]]'' episode "The Thief from Outer Space", he played the Slave to the alien Thief ([[Malachi Throne]]), who threatens the Robinsons.

In ''[[The Beverly Hillbillies]]'' episode "The Dahlia Feud" from 1967, he played Mr. Ted, a large, muscular gardener who plants [[dahlia]]s for Mrs. Drysdale. In 1968, Cassidy appeared on ''[[Mannix]]'' in the episode [[Mannix (season 1)|"To Kill a Writer"]] as Felipe Montoya, on ''[[Daniel Boone (1964 TV series)|Daniel Boone]]'' in "The Scrimshaw Ivory Chart" as a pirate named Gentle Sam, and in two episodes of ''[[I Dream of Jeannie]]'' as the master of Jeannie's devious sister in the episode "Genie, Genie, Who's Got the Genie?", and Jeannie's cousin in the episode "Please Don't Feed the Astronauts".

In the two-part ''[[The Six Million Dollar Man]]'' episode "The Return of [[Bigfoot]]" (1976), Cassidy provided the body and vocal effects of Bigfoot (the role was originally played by professional wrestler [[André the Giant]] in a previous two-parter). Cassidy reprised the role in the 1977 episode "Bigfoot V".

Cassidy also starred in ''[[Bonanza]]'''s "Decision in Los Robles" in 1970.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.fernsehserien.de/bonanza/folgen/11x24-entscheidung-in-los-robles-26128 |title= Bonanza Staffel 11, Folge 24: Entscheidung in Los Robles |date= November 7, 2019 |website= fernsehserien.de |access-date= }}</ref>

===Other film and TV work===
Concurrent with his appearances on ''The Addams Family'', Cassidy began doing character voices on a recurring basis for the [[Hanna-Barbera]] Studios, culminating in the role of Frankenstein Jr., in ''[[Frankenstein Jr. and The Impossibles]]'' series, and even reprising Lurch on several occasions for Hanna-Barbera productions (most notably for the [[The Addams Family (1973 TV series)|''Addams Family'' animated series]] in 1973–74). He was the voice of ''Meteor Man'' in ''[[Birdman and the Galaxy Trio]]'', as well as the hero in the [[Chuck Menville]] pixillated short film ''[[Blaze Glory]]'', in which his already-deep voice was enhanced with reverb echo to give the character an exaggerated super-hero sound. Cassidy also voiced Ben Grimm ("The Thing") in ''[[The New Fantastic Four]]''. Cassidy went on to perform the roars and growls for [[Godzilla]] in the [[Godzilla (animated series)|1979 cartoon series]] that Hanna-Barbera co-produced with [[Toho]], and was also the voice of Montaro in the ''[[Jana of the Jungle]]'' segments that accompanied ''Godzilla'' during its first network run. His voice was the basis for the sinister voice of [[Black Manta]], as well as [[Brainiac]] and several others on ''[[Super Friends]]''. Cassidy was the original voice of [[Moltar]] and [[List of Space Ghost Coast to Coast characters|Metallus]] on ''[[Space Ghost (TV series)|Space Ghost]]'' from 1966 to 1968. Cassidy's final role was as King Thun of the Lion Men in the television animated feature film ''[[Flash Gordon: The Greatest Adventure of All]]''. That particular role was originally recorded shortly before Cassidy's death in 1979, until the decision was made to use the footage for a television series, ''[[The New Adventures of Flash Gordon]]''. As such, Cassidy's death necessitated his role being recast for the series with [[Allan Melvin]]. After the series' conclusion, the original feature film and soundtrack were reassembled using Cassidy's performance and broadcast in prime time in 1982. In live-action productions for the TV series ''The Incredible Hulk'', he provided narration of the title sequence, and the Hulk's growls and roars.<ref name=KOOL>{{cite web |url= http://kool1079.com/10-things-you-didnt-know-about-the-incredible-hulk/ |title= 10 Things You Didn't Know About 'The Incredible Hulk' |author= zanemathews |date= January 22, 2015 |work= kool1079.com |publisher= KOOL 107.9 FM |access-date= }}</ref> In deleted scenes from the original ''[[Battlestar Galactica (1978 TV series)|Battlestar Galactica]]'' TV pilot movie, "[[Saga of a Star World]]", Cassidy can be heard providing temporary voice tracks of the [[Cylon (1978)|Cylon]] [[Imperious Leader]], before actor [[Patrick Macnee]] was contracted to voice the character.<ref>{{cite video |type= DVD |title= Battlestar Galactica: The Complete Epic Series}}</ref>

Other film work includes ''[[Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid]]'' (1969), ''[[Mackenna's Gold]]'' (1969), ''The Limit'' (1972), ''Banacek'' (1972),''[[Black Rage (film)|Charcoal Black]]'' (1972), ''[[The Slams]]'' (1973), ''Thunder County'' (1974), ''[[Poor Pretty Eddie]]'' (1975), ''[[Harry and Walter Go to New York]]'' (1976), ''[[The Last Remake of Beau Geste]]'' (1977) and ''[[Goin' Coconuts]]'' (1978). Alongside Michael Werner, he co-wrote the screenplay of 1973's ''[[The Harrad Experiment]]'', in which he made a brief appearance. During that time, he also worked with [[Noel Marshall]], the executive producer of ''Harrad Experiment'', on the adventure-comedy film ''[[Roar (film)|Roar]]'' (released two years after his death).<ref>{{cite web |url= http://kqek.com/mobile/?p=11643 |title= Film: Roar (1981) |last= Hasan |first= Mark R. |work= KQEK.com |date= June 18, 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190128030645/http://kqek.com/mobile/?p=11643 |archive-date= January 28, 2019 |url-status= live |access-date= January 27, 2019}}</ref>

In 1965, he released a single on [[Capitol Records]] with "The Lurch", written by [[Gary S. Paxton]], and "Wesley", written by [[Cliffie Stone]] and Scott Turner.<ref>{{cite web |title= Ted Cassidy: The Lurch/Wesley |date= September 6, 1965 |website= [[Discogs]] |url= https://www.discogs.com/Ted-Cassidy-The-Lurch-Wesley/release/1853174 |archive-date= May 11, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180511013312/https://www.discogs.com/Ted-Cassidy-The-Lurch-Wesley/release/1853174 |url-status= live |access-date= May 10, 2018}}</ref> He introduced the dance and performed the song "The Lurch" on September 11, 1965, on ''[[Shivaree (TV series)|Shivaree!]]'' and performed it again on Halloween of the same year on ''[[Shindig!]]''<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.cbsnews.com/dfw/news/the-foote-files-remembering-ted-cassidy/ |publisher= [[CBS News]] |title= The Foote Files: Remembering Ted Cassidy |first= Ken |last= Foote |date= May 19, 2017 |archive-date= May 11, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180511013353/http://dfw.cbslocal.com/2017/05/19/the-foote-files-remembering-ted-cassidy/ |url-status= live |access-date= May 10, 2018}}</ref>

==Health issues and death==
Contrary to rumors, and despite being {{height|ft=6|in=9}} tall, Cassidy did not suffer from [[gigantism]].<!-- The previous version of this paragraph mentioned acromegaly. I don't know if that disorder is also involved in an urban legend regarding Ted Cassidy, but in the cited video his son specifically mentions rumors of gigantism, not acromegaly. --> This has been debunked by his son Sean Cassidy.<ref>{{cite web |author= J & B In The Hills |date= 2023-09-06 |title= Sean Cassidy Q & A About His Dad Ted (Lurch) Addams Family, Untrue Rumors |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6cCXeqJ7Eak&t=1842 |website= YouTube |access-date= 2025-12-21}}</ref>

Cassidy underwent surgery at [[St. Vincent Medical Center (Los Angeles)|St. Vincent Medical Center]] in Los Angeles to have a benign tumor removed from his heart. Complications arose several days later while he was recuperating at home. He was readmitted to the same hospital, where he died on January 16, 1979, at age 46. He was cremated and his ashes were buried in the backyard of his home in [[Woodland Hills, Los Angeles|Woodland Hills]].<ref name="obtupi">{{cite news |newspaper= [[The Hour (newspaper)|The Hour]] |location= Norwalk, Connecticut |title= Ted Cassidy's death almost unreported |agency= [[United Press International|UPI]] |date= January 24, 1979 |page= 6 |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=uKs0AAAAIBAJ&pg=5751%2C4125057 |archive-date= September 28, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200928133638/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=uKs0AAAAIBAJ&sjid=Am4FAAAAIBAJ&pg=5751%2C4125057 |url-status= live |access-date= May 13, 2016}}</ref><ref name="delse">{{cite news |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=rBBPAAAAIBAJ&pg=3856%2C1264401 |newspaper= [[Toledo Blade]] |location= Toledo, Ohio |agency= Associated Press |title= Deaths elsewhere: Ted Cassidy |date= January 24, 1979 |page= 12 |archive-date= September 28, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200928133639/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=rBBPAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ggIEAAAAIBAJ&pg=3856%2C1264401 |url-status= live |access-date= May 13, 2016}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> His family had a private funeral service for him at [[Forest Lawn Memorial Park (Hollywood Hills)|Forest Lawn Memorial Park]].<ref>{{cite web |title= Ted Cassidy (The Addams Family) |url= https://findadeath.com/ted-cassidy |website= findadeath.com |access-date= }}</ref>

{{Short description|American sound designer (born 1948)}} {{Use American English|date=July 2022}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2022}} {{Infobox person | name = Ben Burtt | image = Ben Burtt Celebration Europe II.jpg | caption = Burtt at ''Star Wars'' Celebration Europe II in Essen, Germany in 2013 | birth_name = Benjamin Burtt Jr. | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1948|7|12}} | birth_place = [[Jamesville, New York]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | othername = | education = [[Allegheny College]]
[[University of Southern California]] | occupation = {{Flatlist| * [[Sound design]]er * [[film director]] * [[film editing|film editor]] * [[screenwriter]] * [[voice acting|voice actor]] }} | years_active = 1975–present | spouse = | domesticpartner = | awards = {{Flatlist| * Doctor of Arts * Charles S. Swartz Award * Academy Award }} | website = | children = [[Benjamin A. Burtt]] }} '''Benjamin Burtt Jr.''' (born July 12, 1948) is an American [[sound design]]er, [[film director]], [[film editor]], [[screenwriter]], and [[voice acting|voice actor]]. As a sound designer, his credits include the ''[[Star Wars]]'' and ''[[Indiana Jones]]'' film series, ''[[Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978 film)|Invasion of the Body Snatchers]]'' (1978), ''[[E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial]]'' (1982), ''[[WALL-E]]'' (2008), and ''[[Star Trek (2009 film)|Star Trek]]'' (2009). Burtt is notable for popularizing the [[Wilhelm scream]] in-joke and creating many of the iconic sound effects heard in the ''Star Wars'' [[Media franchise|film franchise]], including the 'voice' of [[R2-D2]], the [[lightsaber]] hum, the sound of the blaster guns, the heavy-breathing sound of [[Darth Vader]], and creating the Ewoks’ language, Ewokese. Burtt was also the sound editor for ''WALL-E'' and performed the vocalizations of the character of [[WALL-E (character)|WALL-E]] as well as other robots in the film. Burtt has won four [[Academy Awards]], two of which are [[Special Achievement Academy Award]]s. He has also directed numerous documentary films for [[IMAX]] and most notably the television series [[The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles|''Young Indiana Jones'']] on the episode "Attack of the Hawkmen." He also served as the editor on multiple episodes of the show and the [[Star Wars prequel trilogy|''Star Wars'' prequel trilogy]]. ==Early life== Burtt was born in [[Jamesville, New York]], on July 12, 1948.{{cite book |last1=McGee |first1=Marty |title=Encyclopedia of Motion Picture Sound |date=2001 |publisher=McFarland |location=Jefferson, N.C. |pages=[https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofmo0000mcge/page/52 52]-53 |isbn=9780786410231 |url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofmo0000mcge|url-access=registration }} The son of a chemistry professor at [[Syracuse University]] and a child psychologist, Burtt made films as a child, and later studied [[physics]] at [[Allegheny College]], Pennsylvania, graduating in 1970.{{cite book |last1=Cavin |first1=Andrew I. |editor1-last=Thompson |editor1-first=Clifford |title=Current Biography Yearbook 2003 |date=2003 |publisher=H.W. Wilson |location=New York |isbn=0824210263 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/currentbiography2003thom/page/47 47]-50 |url=https://archive.org/details/currentbiography2003thom |url-access=registration |chapter=Burtt, Ben}} ==Career== ===Early career=== Burtt made films during his time in college, and in 1970 won a National Student Film Festival for his [[war film]] entitled ''Yankee Squadron'', reputedly after following exposure to classic aviation drama.{{Citation needed|date=January 2012}} He had previously made an amateur film at the [[Old Rhinebeck Aerodrome]], a living aviation museum in [[Red Hook, New York|Red Hook]], New York, under guidance from its founder, [[Cole Palen]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2012}} For his work on the special-effects film ''Genesis'', Burtt won a scholarship to the [[University of Southern California]]'','' where he earned a [[master's degree]] in [[Filmmaking|film production]]. ===Sound designer=== Burtt pioneered many aspects of modern sound design, especially in the [[science fiction film|science-fiction]] and [[fantasy film|fantasy-film]] genres.Holman, Tomlinson. ''Sound for Film and Television''. New York: Focal Press, 2010, p. 145. Before his work in the first ''Star Wars'' (now known as ''Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope'') in 1977, science-fiction films tended to use electronic-sounding effects for futuristic devices. Burtt sought a more natural sound, blending in "found sounds" to create the effects. The [[lightsaber]] hum, for instance, was derived from a film projector idling combined with feedback from a broken television set, and the blaster effect started with the sound acquired from hitting a [[guy-wire]] on a [[Radio masts and towers|radio tower]] with a [[hammer]].{{cite web|url=http://filmsound.org/starwars/|title=Sound Design of Star Wars|access-date=March 9, 2014|archive-date=October 11, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181011015556/http://filmsound.org/starwars/|url-status=live}} In the ''Star Wars'' series, part of R2-D2's beeps and whistles are Burtt's vocalizations, also made using an [[ARP 2600]] [[synthesizer]], as are some of the squawks made by the tiny [[hologram|holographic]] monsters on the ''[[Millennium Falcon]]'' [[spacecraft]]. In ''[[Star Wars: Episode III – Revenge of the Sith]]'' (2005), Burtt's provided the voice for Lushros Dofine, captain of the ''[[List of Star Wars spacecraft#Invisible Hand (Providence-class carrier/destroyer)|Invisible Hand]]'' cruiser. The heavy breathing of Darth Vader was created by recording Burtt's own breathing in an old [[Dacor (scuba diving)|Dacor]] [[Diving regulator|scuba regulator]].{{citation needed|date=January 2023}} Burtt used the voice of an elderly lady that he had met in a photography shop for the voice of ''[[E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial]]''. The woman's low pitch was the result of very heavy smoking, specifically Kool cigarettes. Burtt created the "voice" of the title character and many other robots in [[Pixar]]'s film ''[[WALL-E]]'' (2008), about a lonely garbage-compacting robot. Additionally, Burtt is responsible for the sound effects in ''[[Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull]]'' (2008).{{cite web|url=http://trekmovie.com/2009/01/05/star-trek-post-production-complete-oscar-winner-ben-burtt-provided-sound-design/|title=Star Trek Post Production Complete + Oscar-winner Ben Burtt Provided Sound Design|first=Anthony|last=Pascale|date=6 January 2009|work=trekmovie.com|access-date=4 January 2017|archive-date=15 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180615135149/https://trekmovie.com/2009/01/05/star-trek-post-production-complete-oscar-winner-ben-burtt-provided-sound-design/|url-status=live}} Burtt has a reputation for including a sound effect dubbed "the [[Wilhelm scream]]" in many of the movies he has worked on. Taken from a character named "Wilhelm" in the film ''[[The Charge at Feather River]]'', the sound can be heard in a large number of films, including in ''Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope'' when a [[Stormtrooper (Star Wars)|stormtrooper]] falls into a chasm and in ''Raiders of the Lost Ark'' when a [[Nazism|Nazi]] soldier falls off the back of a moving car.{{Cite web |last=Dudley |first=Joshua |date=2023-02-15 |title=Wilhelm Scream: The History of Film’s Most Popular Sound Effect |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/wilhelm-scream-explained-75982/ |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=Backstage |language=en}} One of Burtt's more subtle sound effects is the "audio black hole". In ''[[Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones|Attack of the Clones]]'', Burtt's use of the audio black hole involved the insertion of a short interval of absolute silence in the audio track, just prior to the detonation of "seismic charges" fired at the escaping Jedi spaceship. The effect of this short (less than one second) of silence is to accentuate the resulting explosion in the mind of the listener. Burtt has recalled the source of this idea as follows: "I think back to where that idea might have come to me...I remember in film school a talk I had with an old retired sound editor who said they used to leave a few frames of silence in the track just before a big explosion. In those days they would 'paint' out the optical sound with ink. Then I thought of the airlock entry sequence in ''[[2001: A Space Odyssey (film)|2001]]''. I guess the seeds were there for me to nourish when it came to the seismic charges." Burtt was among the [[golden ear]]s that critically reviewed the various [[data compression|audio compression]] systems that were proposed for the [[ATSC standards|ATSC 1.0]] [[digital television]] system. A tongue-in-cheek homage to Burtt appears in the 1997 [[Activision]] PC game ''[[Zork: Grand Inquisitor]]'' - the [[Magic (paranormal)|spell]] 'Beburtt', which 'creates the illusion of inclement weather', plays dramatic thunderclap and rainfall sounds when cast. ===Director, editor, and writer=== Burtt has directed several [[IMAX]] [[documentary film]]s, including ''[[Blue Planet (1990 film)|Blue Planet]]'', ''[[Destiny in Space]]'', and the [[Academy Awards|Oscar]]-nominated ''[[Special Effects: Anything Can Happen]]''.{{Cite web|url=http://www.filmreference.com/film/92/Ben-Burtt.html|title=Ben Burtt Biography|access-date=October 25, 2008|publisher=NetIndustries, LLC. |year=2008|author=filmreference.com| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080914095700/http://www.filmreference.com/film/92/Ben-Burtt.html| archive-date= 14 September 2008 | url-status= live}} He edited the entire ''Star Wars'' [[Star Wars#Prequel trilogy|prequel trilogy]], and several episodes of ''[[The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles]]''. Burtt also wrote several episodes of the 1980s ''Star Wars'' cartoon ''[[Star Wars: Droids|Droids]]''.{{cite web |last=Greene |first=Jamie |title=Everything you'd ever want to know about Star Wars: Droids |url=https://www.syfy.com/syfywire/everything-youd-ever-want-to-know-about-star-wars-droids |website=SyFy Wire |access-date=April 22, 2020 |date=January 18, 2018 |archive-date=January 20, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190120050018/https://www.syfy.com/syfywire/everything-youd-ever-want-to-know-about-star-wars-droids |url-status=live }} ===Cameo appearances=== Burtt makes a cameo appearance in two of the ''Star Wars'' films as an extra. In ''[[Return of the Jedi]]'', he appeared as Colonel Dyer, the Imperial officer who yells "Freeze!" before [[Han Solo]] knocks him off a balcony. '''Henry Corden''' ({{né}} '''Cohen'''; January 6, 1920 – May 19, 2005) was a Canadian-born American actor, best known for assuming the voice of [[Fred Flintstone]] after the death of [[Alan Reed]] in 1977.<ref name="m">{{cite book| last1=Lawson| first1=Tim| last2=Persons| first2=Alisa| title=The Magic Behind the Voices: A Who's Who of Cartoon Voice Actors| date=December 4, 2004| publisher=Univ. Press of Mississippi| isbn=978-1578066964| page=289| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6ffdBDDBUYsC&q=%22Henry+Corden%22+actor&pg=PA289| access-date=15 August 2017| language=en}}</ref> His official debut as Fred Flintstone was in a 1965 [[Hanna-Barbera]] record, ''Fred Flintstone and Barney Rubble in Songs from Mary Poppins'',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://cartoonresearch.com/index.php/saving-mr-flintstone/ |title=Saving Mr. Flintstone |last=Ehrbar |first=Greg |date=March 18, 2014 |website=Cartoon Research |access-date=July 9, 2025}}</ref> and he also provided the singing voice for Reed in the 1966 theatrical film ''[[The Man Called Flintstone]]'' and the Hanna-Barbera specials ''[[Alice in Wonderland or What's a Nice Kid like You Doing in a Place like This?]]'' (1966) and ''[[Energy: A National Issue]]'' (1977). He took over the role as Fred Flintstone full time in 1977 starting with the syndicated weekday series ''[[Fred Flintstone and Friends]]'' for which he provided voice-overs on brief bumper clips shown in between segments.

==Early years==
Corden was born January 6, 1920,<ref>{{cite book|last=Lentz|first=Harris M.|title=Obituaries in the Performing Arts|location=Jefferson, N.C.|publisher=McFarland & Co.|date=2006|oclc=34483425|page=75}}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=Lentz has published misinformation before.|date=May 2025}} in [[Montreal]] to [[Jewish]] immigrants Max and Emma Cohen.<ref name=LAT/> His father was a meat curer who had been born in Romania; his mother was originally from Russia. The family moved to the [[Bronx]], [[New York (state)|New York]] when Corden was a child and he arrived in [[Hollywood, Los Angeles, California|Hollywood]] in the 1940s.

==Career==
Corden appeared on the stage in Los Angeles, including a 1947 production of ''The Message''. His film career included ''The System'' (1952), where he played a near-sighted gangster named Specs. Corden thought it would be the first time in 25 films he could wear his glasses and see while he was acting, but the lenses gave off too much reflection and he had to substitute them for plain glass after one day of shooting.<ref>The Associated Press, quoted in the ''Spartanburg Herald-Journal'', December 28, 1952.</ref>

Corden's obituary in the ''[[Tampa Bay Times]]'' noted, "With his deep voice, jet-black hair and ethnic looks, Corden was frequently tapped to play heavies in films and on television."[2] He can be seen in such live-action films as [[The Secret Life of Walter Mitty (1947 film)|''The Secret Life of Walter Mitty'']], ''[[The Black Castle]]'', ''[[Abbott and Costello in the Foreign Legion]]'' and [[The Ten Commandments (1956 film)|''The Ten Commandments'']]. He also appeared in dozens of TV shows, including ''[[Hogan's Heroes]]'' (in five episodes), [[Dragnet (1967 TV series)|''Dragnet'']], [[Perry Mason (1957 TV series)|''Perry Mason'']], ''[[Peter Gunn]]'', ''[[McHale's Navy]]'' (in five episodes), ''[[Gunsmoke]]'', ''[[The Mary Tyler Moore Show]]'' and was a regular on ''[[The Jerry Lewis Show]]''. Corden also played landlord Henry Babbitt on ''[[The Monkees (TV series)|The Monkees]]'' and Mr. Haskell, the owner of an ice cream parlor, in an episode of ''[[The Brady Bunch]]''.

Before Reed's death, Corden had been used as Reed's replacement when Fred Flintstone had to sing because Reed could not sing in pitch.<ref name=m/> Corden gave his voice to a number of [[Hanna-Barbera]] productions besides ''[[The Flintstones]]'', including ''[[The Jetsons]]'', ''[[Josie and the Pussycats (TV series)|Josie and the Pussycats]]'', ''The [[Atom Ant]] Show'', and Paw Rugg on [[The Hillbilly Bears]], ''[[Tom and Jerry|The New Tom & Jerry Show]]'' and ''[[Jonny Quest (TV series)|Jonny Quest]]''. Corden also gave voice to the wizard Gemini and Ookla the Mokk in [[Ruby-Spears Productions]]' ''[[Thundarr the Barbarian]]'' as well as the Gorilla General Urko in [[DePatie-Freleng Enterprises]]' ''[[Return to the Planet of the Apes]]''. He voiced Arnie Barkley, the [[Archie Bunker]]-inspired patriarch of DePatie-Freleng's ''[[The Barkleys]]'', in 1972.

==Personal life==
Corden was married four times. His first wife was Thelma Corden, from 1942 to 1969; together they had two children.<ref name=LAT/> He and his second wife Shirley W. Cytron were married from 1970 to 1979. After his divorce from Cytron, he married his third wife Charlotte R. Colton Diamond in 1984; they remained married until her death in 1993. Corden's fourth and final marriage was to Angelina Corden in 1995, and they remained married until Corden's death in 2005.<ref name=LAT>{{cite news| title=Henry Corden, 85; Played Film and TV Heavies, Was Voice of Fred Flintstone| url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2005-may-21-me-corden21-story.html| date=May 21, 2005| newspaper=Los Angeles Times| first=Dennis| last=McLellan}}</ref>
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Henry Corden in The Monkees c. 1967.jpg|thumb|right|Henry Corden in The Monkees c. 1967]] -->

==Death==
Corden died of [[emphysema]] at [[Sherman Oaks Hospital]] in [[Sherman Oaks, California]] on May 19 2005, at the age of 85.<ref name=LAT/> Corden's wife of nine years, Angelina, was with him at the time.

His interment was at [[San Fernando Mission Cemetery]].<ref>{{cite news| title=Henry Corden, 85 Dies; Voice of Fred Flintstone| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/05/21/arts/television/henry-corden-85-dies-voice-of-fred-flintstone.html| newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| date=May 21, 2005| agency=Associated Press| url-access=subscription}}</ref>

'''Janos Prohaska''' (born '''János Prohászka'''; October 10, 1919 – March 13, 1974) was a Hungarian-born American actor and [[stunt performer]]. He appeared on American television from the 1960s and usually played the roles of animals (mostly bears and gorillas) or monsters.

He played a recurring comic role as The Cookie Bear on ''[[The Andy Williams Show]]'' from 1969 to 1971.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Page |first1=Don |title=Janos Prohaska and the Bear Facts on the Cooky Caper |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-janos-prohaska-19/175307740/ |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=February 28, 1971 |location=Los Angeles, CA |page=390 |access-date=June 26, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> Prohaska also appeared in multiple roles on TV series including ''[[The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)|The Outer Limits]]'', ''[[Bewitched]]'', ''[[I Dream of Jeannie]]'', ''[[Lost in Space]]'', and a few episodes of ''[[Gilligan's Island]]'', where he plays a gorilla. His only credited role on that series appears in the episode "Our Vines Have Tender Apes." He also played the title role in the 1965 [[Perry Mason (1957 TV series)|Perry Mason]] episode, "The Case of the Grinning Gorilla". In 1967 he appeared as a white gorilla in the "Fatal Cargo" episode of the ABC-TV sci-fi  series ''[[Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (TV series)|Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea]]''.

He was in the first ''Star Trek'' pilot, [[The Cage (Star Trek: The Original Series)|''The Cage'']], as an ape and as a humanoid bird.<ref name="En1">{{cite book |title=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |first1=Michael |last1=Okuda |author-link1=Michael Okuda |first2=Denise |last2=Okuda |author-link2=Denise Okuda |title-link=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |publisher=Pocket Books |page=717 |isbn=0-671-53609-5 |year=1999}} "Prohaska, Janos: Anthropoid ape and Humanoid bird, 'Cage, The' (TOS); '''Horta'''; '''mugato'''; '''Yarnek''', costumed"</ref> Later he was in three episodes of the [[Star Trek: The Original Series|original ''Star Trek'' series]], wearing alien costumes he himself designed and made as the Horta in "[[The Devil in the Dark]]"<ref name="En2">{{cite book |title=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |first1=Michael |last1=Okuda |author-link1=Michael Okuda |first2=Denise |last2=Okuda |author-link2=Denise Okuda|title-link=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |publisher=Pocket Books |page=187 |isbn=0-671-53609-5 |year=1999}} "'''Horta''' (Janos Prohaska)... The Horta was designed, built, and performed by Janos Prohaska, who reportedly wore the costume into ''Star Trek'' producer [[Gene L. Coon|Gene Coon]]'s office. Coon liked the creature so much he wrote "Devil in the Dark" to feature it."</ref> and the mugato in "[[A Private Little War (TOS episode)|A Private Little War]]".<ref name="En3">{{cite book |title=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |first1=Michael |last1=Okuda |author-link1=Michael Okuda |first2=Denise |last2=Okuda |author-link2=Denise Okuda |title-link=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |publisher=Pocket Books |page=311 |isbn=0-671-53609-5 |year=1999}} "'''mugato''' (Janos Prohaska)... Janos Prohaska was also the '''Horta''' from "Devil in the Dark" and the '''Excalbian''' from "The Savage Curtain"... Prohaska designed and built the ''mugato'' from an ape suit he had previously built for another project."</ref>

He also stunt-doubled for both [[Arnold Stang]] and [[Peter Falk]] in the 1963 film ''[[It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World]]'' in which Stang, a small and lightweight man, wore shoulder pads under his costume so that his appearance would match the bulky appearance of Prohaska.

Prohaska made an appearance on an episode of ''[[What's My Line?]]'' in 1969, where he wore one of his ape costumes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.handitv.com/lists/this-is-the-man-behind-the-mask-of-all-those-60s-and-70s-tv-creatures|title=This is the man behind the mask of all those '60s and '70s TV creatures|website=H&I}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Prohaska was born on October 10, 1919 in [[Budapest]], Hungary. He was married to Irene M. Knoke from June 29, 1969 until his death on March 13, 1974. He and his son Robert were killed along with 34 others in the [[Sierra Pacific Airlines Flight 802|crash]] of a chartered [[Sierra Pacific Airlines]] [[Convair 240|Convair CV-440]] aircraft near [[Bishop, California]], while filming the ABC/Wolper Productions television series ''Primal Man''.<ref>{{cite news |title=Investigators Reach Site of Air Crash |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/ledger-enquirer-janos-prohaska-1919-197/175379543/ |work=Ledger-Enquirer |date=March 15, 1974 |location=Columbus, GA |page=40 |access-date=June 27, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The 'Primal Man' Crash|url=http://www.check-six.com/Crash_Sites/PrimalMan-N4819C.htm|website=Check-Six.com|accessdate=July 16, 2014}}</ref> The plane flew into a mountain ridge in darkness, and the exact cause of the crash was never determined.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=19740313-0|title=ASN Aircraft accident Convair CV-440 N4819C Bishop Airport, CA (BIH)|first=Harro|last=Ranter|website=aviation-safety.net}}</ref> Prohaska was cremated and his ashes were interred in the Mausoleum at [[Woodlawn Memorial Cemetery, Santa Monica]].{{citation needed|date=May 2025}}

'''William Campbell''' (October 30, 1923<ref name=":0">{{cite news |first=Keith |last=Thursby |date=May 1, 2011 |title=Veteran actor had numerous film, TV roles |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2011-may-01-la-me-william-campbell-20110501-story.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230225064729/https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-william-campbell-20110501-story.html |archive-date=February 25, 2023 }}</ref> – April 28, 2011<ref>{{cite news |first=Mike |last=Barnes |url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/star-trek-favorite-william-campbell-183795 |title='Star Trek' Favorite William Campbell Dies at 84 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=April 29, 2011}}</ref>) was an American actor. He played [[supporting actor|supporting]] roles in major [[film]] productions during the 1950s and '60s, and starred in several low-budget [[B-movie]]s and [[horror fiction|horror]] films. He also had several roles in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise.<ref name=":1" />

== Early life ==
Campbell was born in [[Newark, New Jersey]] in 1923. He served in the [[U.S. Navy]] during [[World War II]], on a minesweeper in the Pacific theater.<ref name="Thursby">{{cite news |first=Keith |last=Thursby |date=May 1, 2011 |title=William Campbell dies at 87; actor had numerous film, TV roles |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |url=https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-william-campbell-20110501-story.html}}</ref> He studied acting at the [[HB Studio]], under [[Herbert Berghof]] and [[Uta Hagen]].

==Career==
Campbell's film career began in 1950, with a small part in the [[John Garfield]] film ''[[The Breaking Point (1950 film)|The Breaking Point]].'' After several years of similar supporting performances in a number of films, including as a co-pilot in [[William Wellman]]'s ''[[The High and the Mighty (film)|The High and the Mighty]]'' (1954), he won his first starring role in ''[[Cell 2455 Death Row (film)|Cell 2455 Death Row]]'' (1955), a low-budget prison film for [[Columbia Pictures]]. He played a [[death row]] inmate, based loosely on the true story of [[Caryl Chessman]], who staunchly proclaimed his innocence and obtained numerous reprieves over many years until finally being executed. Campbell's surprisingly powerful performance received generally good notices from critics, but it did very little for his career;{{Citation needed |date=September 2024}} his next several roles were again providing support to lead actors, including ''[[Man Without a Star]]'' (1955), ''[[Love Me Tender (1956 film)|Love Me Tender]]'' (1956)  in which he became the first person to lip sync portions of a song onscreen (actually recorded on August 24, 1956, by the Ken Darby Trio){{Citation needed |date=September 2024}} with [[Elvis Presley]], and [[The Naked and the Dead (film)|the 1958 film version]] of [[Norman Mailer]]'s ''[[The Naked and the Dead]].  ''

In 1958, Campbell co-starred with [[Paul Birch (actor)|Paul Birch]] in ''[[Cannonball (series)|Cannonball]]'',<ref>{{cite news |title=TV Notes |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/santa-barbara-news-press-william-campbel/172603105/ |work=[[Santa Barbara News-Press]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=July 19, 1958 |page=14 |access-date=May 18, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> a short-lived [[television series]] about truck drivers. After that, he worked for more years in small parts in increasingly lower grade movies.

Campbell made two guest appearances on ''[[Perry Mason (1957 TV series)|Perry Mason]]'' in 1959 and 1960. In his first appearance he played the title character and murder victim Allen Sheridan in "The Case of the Artful Dodger," then he played murderer and title character Jim Ferris in "The Case of the Ill-Fated Faker."

In 1963, Campbell began a brief association with [[Roger Corman]], starring in the director's ''[[The Young Racers]]'' that year. The auto-racing-themed movie, written for the screen by Campbell's brother [[Robert Wright Campbell]], was shot in Ireland. After production was completed, the film's sound man, [[Francis Ford Coppola]], talked Corman into allowing Coppola to remain in Ireland with a small crew and direct a low-budget horror film, to be produced by Corman. Coppola promised it would be the cheapest film Corman was ever involved in. Shot for approximately $40,000, the resultant film, ''[[Dementia 13]]'' (1963), was an atmospheric and violent horror thriller clearly made in imitation of ''[[Psycho (1960 film)|Psycho]]''.{{Citation needed |date=September 2024}} Campbell starred as a moody loner who at one point becomes the chief suspect in a series of gruesome axe killings; [[Patrick Magee (actor)|Patrick Magee]] and [[Luana Anders]] led the supporting cast. Many years later, Campbell would provide an [[audio commentary]] for the film's [[DVD]] release.

Campbell also starred in another Corman-produced horror yarn. Filmed in 1963 in [[Yugoslavia]] under the title ''Operacija Ticijan'', again with Magee in the cast, the film was never released in its original form. It was re-edited, re-dubbed, and briefly shown on television as ''Portrait in Terror''. Years later, additional footage was shot in California, first by [[Jack Hill]], then by [[Stephanie Rothman]], transforming what was once a spy thriller into the story of a [[vampire]] stalking the streets of [[Venice, California]]. Retitled ''[[Blood Bath]],'' although it also became known as ''Track of the Vampire'', the film received a limited theatrical release in 1966. Campbell also filmed ''[[The Secret Invasion]]'' in Yugoslavia, directed by Roger Corman and written by his brother Robert Wright Campbell.  Campbell was the only one of the team of commandos not given screen credit above the title.

One year previously in 1965 he landed a supporting role as a reporter in the classic suspense horror; ''[[Hush...Hush, Sweet Charlotte]]''. In ''Blood Bath'' Campbell's character was an artist who killed women and hid their bodies inside his sculptures; he is also a vampire who can freely walk during the daylight in search of victims. However, the fanged vampire was confusingly played by another actor who did not resemble Campbell. Like ''Dementia 13'', the film has managed to develop a following despite its deficiencies. In the early 1990s, ''[[Video Watchdog]]'' magazine devoted lengthy articles in three separate issues painstakingly detailing the convoluted production history of this strange but fascinating movie.

Campbell had guest-starring roles in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise, appearing first as the mischievous super-being [[List of Star Trek characters (T–Z)#T|Trelane]] in an episode of [[Star Trek: The Original Series|the original series]] called "[[The Squire of Gothos]]".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Spelling |first1=Ian |title=Characters Cling On to 'Blood Oath' |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/ventura-county-star-william-campbell-19/172602615/ |work=[[Ventura County Star]] |agency=[[New York Times Syndicate]] |date=March 18, 1994 |page=92 |access-date=May 18, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> Campbell also appeared twice as the [[Klingon]] Captain [[Koloth]]. Campbell first played Koloth on the original ''Star Trek'' series in the episode "[[The Trouble with Tribbles]]". He reprised the role on the series ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' episode entitled "[[Blood Oath (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Blood Oath]]", some thirty years later.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |date=March 11, 2021 |first=Laurie |last=Ulster |title=13 Original Series Actors Who Couldn't Get Enough Trek |url=https://www.startrek.com/news/13-tos-actors-who-appeared-on-other-tv-treks-decades-later |website=StarTrek.com}}</ref> Campbell appeared at several Trek conventions in the 1980s and 1990s. His last appearance was at the convention organized by [[Creation Entertainment]] at the [[Las Vegas Hilton]] in August 2006.

After retiring from acting, Campbell worked for the [[Motion Picture & Television Fund]] as its chief fundraiser.<ref name=":0" />

==Personal life==
Campbell was married twice. His first marriage was to [[Judith Exner]] in 1952. They divorced in 1958.<ref name="Thursby" /> He married Tereza in 1963. They were married until his death.<ref name="Thursby" />

Campbell is a relative of [[Jeff Janiak]], vocalist of the band [[Discharge (band)|Discharge]].<ref>{{cite web |first=Luxi |last=Lahtinen |title=Soundtracks of My Youth – Part Three |url=https://www.metalcrypt.com/pages/features.php?featureid=58 |website=The Metal Crypt |access-date=March 26, 2021}}</ref>

=== Death ===
Campbell died on April 28, 2011, at the [[Motion Picture & Television Country House and Hospital]] in [[Woodland Hills, California]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://startrek.com/article/remembering-william-campbell |title=Remembering William Campbell |website=StarTrek.com |date=April 29, 2011}}</ref>

'''Judith Therese Evans''' (born July 20, 1975), known professionally as '''Judy Greer''', is an American actress. She is primarily known as a [[character actress]] who has appeared in [[Judy Greer filmography|a wide variety of films]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Bramesco |first=Charles |work=[[Nylon (magazine)|Nylon]] |url=https://nylon.com/articles/judy-greer-joy-frustration-character-actress |title=Fact: Judy Greer Is the Best Person in Hollywood |date=March 28, 2017 |access-date=September 19, 2018}}</ref> She rose to prominence for her supporting roles in the films ''[[Jawbreaker (film)|Jawbreaker]]'' (1999), ''[[What Women Want]]'' (2000), ''[[13 Going on 30]]'' (2004), ''[[Elizabethtown (film)|Elizabethtown]]'' (2005), ''[[27 Dresses]]'' (2008), and ''[[Love & Other Drugs]]'' (2010).

Greer expanded into multiple genres with roles in films such as ''[[The Wedding Planner]]'' (2001), ''[[Adaptation (film)|Adaptation]]'' (2002), ''[[The Village (2004 film)|The Village]]'' (2004), ''[[The Descendants]]'' (2011), ''[[Jeff, Who Lives at Home]]'' (2011), ''[[Carrie (2013 film)|Carrie]]'' (2013), ''[[Men, Women & Children (film)|Men, Women & Children]]'' (2014), ''[[Grandma (2015 film)|Grandma]]'' (2015), ''[[Lemon (2017 film)|Lemon]]'' (2017), ''[[Where'd You Go, Bernadette (film)|Where'd You Go, Bernadette]]'' (2019), ''[[Uncle Frank (film)|Uncle Frank]]'' (2020), and ''[[Hollywood Stargirl]]'' (2022). She appeared in numerous [[blockbuster (entertainment)|blockbusters]], such as ''[[Dawn of the Planet of the Apes]]'' (2014) its sequel ''[[War for the Planet of the Apes]]'' (2017), ''[[Jurassic World]]'' (2015), ''[[Halloween (2018 film)|Halloween]]'' (2018) its sequel ''[[Halloween Kills]]'' (2021), and the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] films ''[[Ant-Man (film)|Ant-Man]]'' (2015), ''[[Ant-Man and the Wasp]]'' (2018), and ''[[Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3]]'' (2023).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kit |first=Borys |date=April 3, 2014 |title=Judy Greer Joins 'Jurassic World' |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/judy-greer-joins-jurassic-world-693459/ |access-date=April 11, 2022 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Davids |first=Brian |date=October 16, 2021 |title='Halloween Kills' Stars Judy Greer and Andi Matichak on the Ending: "It's a Bummer" |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/halloween-kills-ending-explained-stars-1235032341/ |access-date=April 11, 2022 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref> She made her directorial debut with the comedy-drama film ''[[A Happening of Monumental Proportions]]'' (2017).

On television, Greer is best known for her starring voice role as [[Cheryl Tunt]] in the [[FXX]] animated comedy series ''[[Archer (2009 TV series)|Archer]]'' (2009–2023) and as Lina Bowman in the [[FX (TV channel)|FX]] sitcom ''[[Married (TV series)|Married]]'' (2014–2015). She also appeared in the comedy series ''[[The Big Bang Theory]]'' (2010), ''[[Arrested Development]]'' (2003–2006, 2013–2019), ''[[Two and a Half Men]]'' (2003–2015), ''[[It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia]]'' (2007–2011), ''[[Kidding]]'' (2018–2020), ''[[Let's Go Luna!]]'' (2018–2022), and ''[[Reboot (2022 TV series)|Reboot]]'' (2022).

==Early life==
Greer was born in [[Detroit]], Michigan, on July 20, 1975.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/entertainment/article/judy-greer-laments-rom-com-decline-while-promoting-new-book/ |title=Judy Greer laments rom-com decline while promoting new book |website=CTV News |date=April 9, 2014 |access-date=April 21, 2014 |first=Victoria |last=Ahearn}}</ref><ref name=allmovie>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/235491/Judy-Greer/biography |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141214044034/http://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/235491/Judy-Greer/biography |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 14, 2014 |title=Judy Greer; Alternate Name: Judy Evans Greer, Judith Laura Evans, Judy Evans, Judith Laura Evans |first=Andrea |last=LeVasseur |department=Movies & TV Dept. |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=2014 |access-date=September 26, 2014}}</ref> Her mother, Mollie Ann (''née'' Greer), is a hospital administrator, and her father, Rich Evans, is a mechanical engineer.{{sfn|Greer|2014|p=25}}<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2012/dec/27/judy-greer-arrested-development-get-flashed |title=Judy Greer: 'I get flashed all the time. It's mostly men' |newspaper=The Guardian |date=December 27, 2012 |first=Hermione |last=Hoby}}</ref> Her mother was once a nun, who was "kicked out" of the convent after eight years for wild behavior, including owning a red bathing suit.<ref name="colbert2017">{{cite news |title=Judy Greer Starred Alongside Stephen In A Rejected 2002 Pilot |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NZ05TIoEYUM |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211030/NZ05TIoEYUM |archive-date=October 30, 2021 |access-date=June 16, 2017 |work=[[The Late Show with Stephen Colbert]] |date=June 16, 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Greer was raised [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]]<ref name=wsj>{{cite web |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/behind-the-scenes-with-judy-greer-1400285798 |title=Behind the Scenes with Judy Greer |last=Wolfe |first=Alexandra |date=May 16, 2014 |access-date=September 19, 2018}} {{closed access}}</ref> and grew up in [[Redford, Michigan|Redford Township]] and [[Livonia, Michigan|Livonia]].<ref name=krug/> She attended [[Winston Churchill High School (Wayne County, Michigan)|Churchill High School]],<ref name=krug>{{cite web |work=[[Metro Times|The Metro Times]] |location=Detroit |url=https://www.metrotimes.com/news-hits/archives/2014/10/23/livonia-native-judy-greer-on-films-tv-and-her-new-book |title=Livonia native Judy Greer on films, TV, and her new book |last=Krug |first=Kurt Anthony |date=October 23, 2014 |access-date=April 23, 2026}}</ref> where she was a part of the Creative and Performing Arts Program and graduated from [[The Theatre School at DePaul University]] in 1997 with a [[Bachelor of Fine Arts]] degree.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://theatreschool.depaul.edu/special_programs_awards.php |title=Awards For Excellence In The Arts |date=May 4, 2006 |website=The Theater School at DePaul University |access-date=July 30, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 13, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060813042958/http://theatreschool.depaul.edu/special_programs_awards.php}}</ref> She later adopted her mother's maiden name for her stage name, as several other actresses are named Judy or Judi Evans.

==Career==
===1997–2003===
Greer made her film debut in the horror film ''Stricken'' (1998), as a college student involved in a fatal prank.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/stricken/ |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |title=Stricken (1998) |access-date=September 17, 2018}}</ref> This was followed by a small role in the Chicago-filmed drama ''[[Kissing a Fool]]'' (1998). She was cast in her first major role as Fern Mayo, a nerdy teenager who uncovers her classmates' murder of their friend, in [[Darren Stein]]'s black comedy ''[[Jawbreaker (film)|Jawbreaker]]'' (1999).<ref name=jb>{{cite web |work=[[Vice Media|Broadly]] |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/perverting-the-youth-of-america-the-oral-history-of-teen-classic-jawbreaker/ |title='Perverting the Youth of America': The Oral History of Teen Classic 'Jawbreaker' |date=August 14, 2016 |access-date=September 19, 2018 |last=Sunderland |first=Mitchell}}</ref> Greer followed this with small parts in the romantic comedy films, ''[[What Women Want]]'' (2000)<ref>{{cite web |work=[[BBC One]] |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b0074dkr |title=What Women Want |access-date=April 23, 2026}}</ref> and ''[[The Wedding Planner]]'' (2001).<ref name=talks>{{cite magazine |url=https://ew.com/article/2015/10/01/judy-greer-married-memorable-roles/ |date=October 1, 2015 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |title=Judy Greer talks 'Arrested Development,' '13 Going on 30,' 'The Descendants,' 'The Wedding Planner,' and more... |last=Li |first=Shirley |access-date=September 19, 2018}}</ref> She was cast in a 2002 pilot for NBC alongside [[Stephen Colbert]], ''Untitled Ken Finkleman Project'' ([[Imagine Entertainment]]), based on the Canadian show ''[[The Newsroom (Canadian TV series)|The Newsroom]]'' from [[Ken Finkleman]]. Colbert portrayed Finkleman and Greer played his sister.<ref name="colbert2017"/>

Greer had a recurring role on the [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]] comedy series ''[[Arrested Development]]'' (2003–2005, 2013, 2018), playing [[List of Arrested Development characters|Kitty Sanchez]] in ten episodes total and appearing in each of the series' three original seasons. In a 2009 interview, she said that she is most recognized for this role.<ref name="goldman">{{cite web |url=http://tv.ign.com/articles/101/1014154p1.html |title=Judy Greer Gets Animated with Glenn Martin, DDS and Archer |access-date=July 30, 2010 |last=Goldman |first=Eric |date=August 14, 2009 |website=IGN}}</ref> She also had a supporting role in ''[[Adaptation (film)|Adaptation]]'' (2002).

===2004–2010===
In 2004, Greer co-starred in the romantic comedy ''[[13 Going on 30]]'', starring [[Jennifer Garner]] as a girl who wakes up one morning as a 30-year-old woman. Greer played Lucy, an untrustworthy fellow editor of Garner's at a fashion magazine where both work.<ref>{{cite news |title="13 Going on 30" Gets Underway |url=http://movies.about.com/cs/upcomingreleases/a/13goingnews.htm |access-date=October 28, 2014 |website=[[About.com]] |date=May 13, 2003 |archive-date=September 22, 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050922165433/http://movies.about.com/cs/upcomingreleases/a/13goingnews.htm |url-status=dead}}</ref> The film was a commercial success, grossing $96.5 million worldwide, and received positive reviews from critics.<ref>{{cite web |title=13 Going on 30 (2004) |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=13goingon30.htm |website=[[Box Office Mojo]] |access-date=September 9, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/13_going_on_30 |title=13 Going on 30 (2004) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |access-date=January 1, 2021}}</ref> Greer had a supporting role in [[M. Night Shyamalan]]'s thriller film ''[[The Village (2004 film)|The Village]]'', about a village whose population lives in fear of creatures inhabiting the woods beyond it. Despite mixed reviews, the film was a success at the box office, grossing $256.7 million worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/village |title=The Village (2004) |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |access-date=October 20, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=village.htm |title=The Village (2004) |website=[[Box Office Mojo]]}}</ref> Greer then played another supporting role in [[Jenna Fischer]]'s directorial debut, the comedy ''[[LolliLove]]'', which premiered at the [[St. Louis International Film Festival]] to positive reviews from critics, though it was ultimately released straight-to-DVD.<ref>{{cite news |title=St. Louis theaters become an import-export market |last=Williams |first=Joe |department=Talking Pictures |newspaper=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]] (MO) |date=March 18, 2005 |page=E1 |url=http://docs.newsbank.com/g/GooglePM/SL/lib00170,108F399CC06A405F.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130129204033/http://docs.newsbank.com/g/GooglePM/SL/lib00170,108F399CC06A405F.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 29, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Bill |last=Gibron |date=February 9, 2006 |title=DVD Talk Review: LolliLove |url=https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/read.php?ID=20095 |website=DVD Talk |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061009161528/https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/read.php?ID=20095 |archive-date=October 9, 2006}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=February 7, 2006 |first=Christopher |last=Curry |title=LolliLove (DVD) |website=[[Film Threat]] |url=https://www.filmthreat.com/reviews/8614/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110711003748/https://www.filmthreat.com/reviews/8614/ |archive-date=July 11, 2011}}</ref>

In 2005, Greer first played a female werewolf in [[Wes Craven]]'s horror film ''[[Cursed (2005 film)|Cursed]]'', starring [[Christina Ricci]] and [[Jesse Eisenberg]]. The film was a failure at the box office and was widely panned by critics, with Craven later expressing disappointment in the film.<ref>{{cite web |author=Capone |url=http://www.aintitcool.com/node/37854 |title=Wes Craven talks to Capone about 25/8, remakes, and the 'Cursed' experience of revisiting old franchises!! |website=Ain't It Cool News |date=March 1, 2009 |access-date=September 2, 2017}}</ref> Greer then starred in the comedy-drama ''[[The Great New Wonderful]]'', which depicts the lives of several New Yorkers one year after the [[September 11th attacks]]. In her character's vignette, Greer played a woman struggling to keep her marriage together. The film premiered at the [[Tribeca Film Festival]] to mostly positive reviews.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/great_new_wonderful/ |title=''The Great New Wonderful'' (2005) |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> Ty Burr of the ''Boston Globe'' called the film "an actor's playpen", and remarked that "Greer has been stuck so long in goofball supporting roles that she tears into this part – a smart, loving mother frightened of her own son – as if it were prime rib."<ref>{{cite web |last=Burr |first=Ty |url=https://archive.boston.com/ae/movies/articles/2006/06/23/wonderful_is_a_quietly_rich_post_911_study/ |title='Wonderful' is a quietly rich post-9/11 study |work=Boston Globe |date=June 23, 2006 |access-date=July 5, 2021}}</ref> Following an appearance in the drama ''[[In Memory of My Father]]'', Greer featured in [[Cameron Crowe]]'s tragic-romantic comedy ''[[Elizabethtown (film)|Elizabethtown]]'', starring [[Orlando Bloom]], [[Kirsten Dunst]], [[Alec Baldwin]] and [[Susan Sarandon]]. The film premiered at the [[Venice International Film Festival]] and garnered negative reviews from critics.<ref>{{cite web |title=Elizabethtown (2005) |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/elizabethtown |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |location=San Francisco, California |language=en |access-date=February 12, 2021}}</ref>

===2011–2014===
In 2011, Greer first starred in the crime thriller ''[[The Key Man (2011 film)|The Key Man]]'', as the wife of a salesman who becomes involved in an insurance scam. The film premiered at South by Southwest.<ref>{{cite web |title=Meet the 2011 SXSW Filmmakers: "The Key Man" Director Peter Himmelstein |date=March 10, 2011 |website=[[IndieWire]] |url=https://www.indiewire.com/2011/03/meet-the-2011-sxsw-filmmakers-the-key-man-director-peter-himmelstein-243365/ |access-date=March 24, 2018}}</ref> Though Seth Freilich of ''Pajiba'' considered Greer to be "lovely as always", he felt that she was "underused", and called for the film industry to offer her better roles.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pajiba.com/film_reviews/the-key-man-review-theres-a-sucker-born-every-minute.php |title=The Key Man Review: There's A Sucker Born Every Minute |last=Freilich |first=Seth |work=Pajiba |date=March 8, 2011 |access-date=July 4, 2021}}</ref> Greer starred in [[Alexander Payne]]'s film ''[[The Descendants]]'', alongside [[George Clooney]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Jason |last=Guerrasio |title=Alexander Payne's 'The Descendants' Begins Shooting |url=http://filmmakermagazine.com/news/2010/03/alexander-paynes-the-descendants-begins-shooting/ |work=[[Filmmaker (magazine)|Filmmaker]] |date=March 15, 2010 |access-date=October 29, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100323033843/http://filmmakermagazine.com/news/2010/03/alexander-paynes-the-descendants-begins-shooting/ |archive-date=March 23, 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> Greer played a woman who discovers that her husband had an extramarital affair with the now-comatose wife of the attorney. The film premiered at the [[Telluride Film Festival]] to critical acclaim.<ref name="variety09072011">{{cite news |url=https://variety.com/2011/film/news/descendants-gets-earlier-bow-1118042405/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110915221329/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1118042405 |archive-date=September 15, 2011 |date=September 7, 2011 |access-date=September 15, 2011 |title='Descendants' gets earlier bow: Clooney starrer beats Thanksgiving glut with Nov. 18 rollout |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |first=Rachel |url-status=live |last=Abrams}}</ref> Greer herself received particularly strong reviews for her performance; David Thomson of ''The New Republic'' found Greer to be "touching", while Philip Kemp of ''Sight & Sound'' praised Greer for turning "her few brief scenes [...] into a moving portrayal of undeservedly broken trust."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Thomson |first=David |url=https://newrepublic.com/article/97757/the-descendents-george-clooney-alexander-payne |title=David Thomson on Films: A Mainstream Movie for People Tired of Noise and Violence |magazine=The New Republic |date=November 24, 2011 |access-date=July 4, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Kemp |first=Philip |url=http://old.bfi.org.uk/sightandsound/review/6771 |title=Film of the month: The Descendants |work=Sight & Sound |date=February 2012 |access-date=July 4, 2021 |archive-date=July 11, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711030357/http://old.bfi.org.uk/sightandsound/review/6771 |url-status=dead}}</ref> For her performance in the film, Greer received nominations for the [[Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by a Cast in a Motion Picture]] and the [[Satellite Award for Best Supporting Actress – Motion Picture]].<ref name="Pond">{{cite web |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-sagensemble-rules/sag-ensemble-rule-rewards-stars-shortchanges-key-actors-idUSTRE7BG02Q20111217 |work=Reuters |title=SAG ensemble rule rewards stars, shortchanges key actors |last=Pond |first=Steve |date=December 16, 2011 |access-date=September 17, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pressacademy.com/award_cat/2011/ |title=2011 Satellite Awards |website=International Press Academy |access-date=April 28, 2016}}</ref>

Following a role in the critically panned romantic comedy ''[[Playing for Keeps (2012 film)|Playing for Keeps]]'', starring [[Gerard Butler]], Greer made her [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] debut in [[Theresa Rebeck]]'s comedy ''[[Dead Accounts]]'', alongside [[Katie Holmes]], [[Norbert Leo Butz]], [[Jayne Houdyshell]] and [[Josh Hamilton (actor)|Josh Hamilton]] (both 2012).<ref>{{cite web |title=Playing for Keeps |url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/playing_for_keeps_2012/ |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=June 28, 2020}}</ref><ref>Judy Greer Biography on [http://broadway.com broadway.com]</ref> The play received negative reviews, with [[Ben Brantley]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' criticizing Greer for not "transcend[ing] her character's function as a visitor-from-another-planet plot device."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/11/30/theater/reviews/dead-accounts-with-katie-holmes-at-music-box-theater.html |title='Dead Accounts' With Katie Holmes at Music Box Theater |first=Ben |last=Brantley |newspaper=The New York Times |date=November 30, 2012 |access-date=April 15, 2017}}</ref> In ''[[Carrie (2013 film)|Carrie]]'' (2013), starring [[Chloë Grace Moretz]] and [[Julianne Moore]], Greer played [[Rita Desjardin|Miss Desjardin]], a gym teacher who becomes involved with the titular character (Moretz), a shy high-school student and outcast, who secretly possesses telekinesis.<ref>{{cite web |last=Miska |first=Brad |url=https://bloody-disgusting.com/news/3145093/judy-greer-in-talks-for-gym-teacher-role-in-carrie-reboot/ |title=Judy Greer In Talks For Gym Teacher Role In 'Carrie' Reboot! |work=BloodyDisgusting.com |date=May 25, 2012 |access-date=July 4, 2021}}</ref> The film, which serves as an adaptation of [[Carrie (novel)|Stephen King's 1974 novel of the same name]] and a re-make of [[Carrie (1976 film)|Brian de Palma's 1976 film]], received mixed reviews from critics, who considered it to be an "unnecessary" adaptation.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://rottentomatoes.com/m/carrie/ |title=Carrie (2013) Reviews |website=Rotten Tomatoes |publisher=Fandango |date=October 18, 2013 |access-date=July 4, 2021}}</ref> Nevertheless, Michael Phillips of the ''Chicago Tribune'', who gave the film a positive review, remarked, "The acting's strong; in addition to Moretz and Moore, Judy Greer is a welcome presence in the [...] role of the sympathetic gym instructor."<ref>{{cite web |last=Phillips |first=Michael |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/la-et-mn-carrie-remake-with-chloe-grace-moretz-divides-critics-20131018-story.html |title=Carrie Remake a Bloody Good Time |work=Chicago Tribune |access-date=July 4, 2021}}</ref>

That same year, Greer made her directorial debut with the [[AOL]] short film ''Quiet Time'', which focuses on how [[transcendental meditation]] can be used for stress relief. ===2015–2018===

That same year, Greer made her feature-film directorial debut in the comedy-drama ''[[A Happening of Monumental Proportions]]'', which depicts one day in the lives of students and staff at a Los Angeles private school. In an interview with ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'', Greer discussed her motivations towards making the film: "I wanted to tell a story where adults act like kids and kids act like adults [...] As I age I'm noticing that more and more, as we see our kids pointing things out to us that we really should know ourselves, you start to realize that you and your adult friends are king of acting like idiots sometimes. We're regressing, clawing at the walls as if to say, I don't want to grow up."<ref>{{cite web |last=Saval |first=Malina |url=https://variety.com/2017/film/news/judy-greer-a-happening-of-monumental-proportions-1202410554/ |title=Judy Greer Talks Directing for the First Time and How to Find a Story to Tell |work=Variety |date=May 5, 2017 |access-date=June 29, 2021}}</ref> The film stars [[Allison Janney]], [[Katie Holmes]], [[Bradley Whitford]], [[Jennifer Garner]] (Greer's co-star from ''13 Going on 30'') and rapper [[Common (rapper)|Common]], received largely negative reviews from critics.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/a_happening_of_monumental_proportions |title=A Happening of Monumental Proportions (2018) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=July 13, 2020}}</ref>

In 2018, Greer first played a supporting role in [[Clint Eastwood]]'s biographical film ''[[The 15:17 to Paris]]'', as the mother of U.S. Air Force Staff Sergeant [[Spencer Stone]]. As part of an overall negative response, Tim Grierson of ''ScreenDaily'' lamented that Greer and co-star [[Jenna Fischer]] were "trapped playing supportive-parent clichés."<ref>{{cite web |last=Grierson |first=Tim |url=https://www.screendaily.com/reviews/the-1517-to-paris-review/5126349.article |title='The 15:17 To Paris': Review |work=ScreenDaily |date=February 7, 2018 |access-date=June 29, 2021}}</ref> Greer followed with [[Jim Loach]]'s comedy-drama ''[[Measure of a Man (film)|Measure of a Man]]''. ==Personal life==
[[File:Judy Greer July 14, 2014 (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|upright|100px|Greer in July 2014]]
In 2011, Greer married Dean E. Johnsen, an executive producer of ''[[Real Time with Bill Maher]]'', becoming the stepmother to his two children from an earlier marriage.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.usmagazine.com/celebrity-news/news/actress-judy-greer-marries-dean-johnson-20111912 |title=Actress Judy Greer Marries Dean Johnsen |first=Zach |last=Johnson |date=December 19, 2011 |website=US magazine |access-date=February 1, 2012}}</ref>

Greer grew up Catholic, although at the age of 10 in 1985, she convinced her parents to let her go to a Presbyterian church, claiming that she thought she would be closer to God there. The real reason was that she thought the boys were cuter at that church.<ref name="colbert2017"/> In 2014, Greer stated that she was no longer a Catholic.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://interviewly.com/i/judy-greer-apr-2014-reddit |title=Interviewly -Judy Greer April 2014 – reddit AMA |work=Interviewly |access-date=April 28, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160428092723/http://interviewly.com/i/judy-greer-apr-2014-reddit |archive-date=April 28, 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2014, she told ''[[Glamour (magazine)|Glamour]]'', "I had been wanting to try to learn how to meditate, and I did research on the different types of meditation. [[Transcendental Meditation technique|TM]] seemed the easiest, and I liked that it wasn't religious in any way."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.glamour.com/story/judy-greer-has-the-perfect-sol |title=Judy Greer Has the Perfect Solution for Coping With Stress in Her New AOL Short |last=Radloff |first=Jessica |work=Glamour |date=May 5, 2014 |access-date=October 7, 2020}}</ref>

Greer is a member of the board of directors of [[Project Chimps]], a sanctuary for former research chimpanzees.<ref>[https://projectchimps.org/about/board-of-directors/ Board of Directors], Project Chimps, accessed November 15, 2022</ref>

She is a registered [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Judy Greer Does The Michigan Minute! |url=https://michigandems.com/hometown-pride-famous-michiganders-connect-with-voters-in-their-hometown/ |date=October 29, 2020 |website=Michigan Democratic Party |access-date=May 12, 2021}}</ref>
