'''Atlantis''' (born September 28, 1962) is a Mexican [[professional wrestling|professional wrestler]] signed to [[Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre]] (CMLL). One of the longest-tenured wrestlers in CMLL history, his [[ring name]] is derived from [[Atlantis|the fabled city]]. His real name is not a matter of public record, as is often the case with [[Wrestling mask|masked]] wrestlers in Mexico, where their private lives are kept a secret from the wrestling fans.<ref name="Mondo">{{cite book|author=Madigan, Dan|title=Mondo Lucha A Go-Go: the bizarre and honorable world of wild Mexican wrestling|publisher=HarperCollins Publishers|year=2007|chapter=Okay... what is Lucha Libre?|pages=29–40|isbn=978-0-06-085583-3}}</ref>

Trained by [[Diablo Velasco]], Atlantis made his in-ring debut in 1983 and has since held a large number of professional wrestling championships, including the [[CMLL World Light Heavyweight Championship]], [[CMLL World Tag Team Championship]], [[CMLL World Trios Championship]], [[Mexican National Light Heavyweight Championship]], [[Mexican National Middleweight Championship]], [[Mexican National Tag Team Championship]], [[Mexican National Trios Championship]], [[NWA World Light Heavyweight Championship]] and [[NWA World Middleweight Championship]]. He has also won the masks of several prominent wrestlers including [[Arturo Beristain|Talismán]], [[Kung Fu (wrestler)|Kung Fu]], [[Villano III]], [[Último Guerrero]] and [[Andrade El Idolo|La Sombra]]. Outside of CMLL, Atlantis has wrestled in Japan for [[New Japan Pro-Wrestling]] (NJPW) and [[Michinoku Pro Wrestling]], where he won the [[Tohoku Junior Heavyweight Championship]], and in the United States for [[World Championship Wrestling]] (WCW), [[Chikara (professional wrestling)|Chikara]], [[Ring of Honor]] (ROH) and [[Major League Wrestling]] (MLW).

Atlantis earned the nickname ''El idolo de los Niños'' (the "Children's Idol") as he was always a favorite with the younger fans. He even retained the nickname when he worked as a ''rudo'' ([[Heel (professional wrestling)|heel]] or "bad guy" character) for several years as part of ''[[Los Guerreros Laguneros|Los Guerreros de la Atlantida]]''. He starred in several [[Luchador films|lucha films]] in the 1990s, including one in which he co-starred with [[Octagón]]: ''Octagón y Atlantis, la revancha'' ("Octagón and Atlantis, the rematch"). 

==Professional wrestling career==
=== Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre (1983–present) ===
==== El idolo de los Niños (1983–2005) ====
He made his professional wrestling debut on June 12, 1983, after training for under a year with world-renowned Mexican wrestling trainer [[Diablo Velasco]].<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" /> He adopted the [[Wrestling mask|masked]] ''tecnico'' ([[Face (professional wrestling)|face]]) [[ring name|ring persona]] of "Atlantis", a supposed warrior from the lost city of [[Atlantis]], donning a mask with an image of two fish, becoming a regular for [[Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre|Empresa Mexicana de Lucha Libre]] (EMLL).<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" /> On November 30, 1984, he defeated [[Jerry Estrada]] to win the [[Mexican National Middleweight Championship]], the first title of his career, holding it for 457 days until losing to [[Arturo Beristain|Talismán]] on March 2, 1986.<ref name="MexMiddle" /><ref name="Lucha2000">{{cite news|title=Los Reyes de Mexico: La Historia de Los Campeonatos Nacionales|work=Lucha 2000|id=Especial 21|date=December 20, 2004|language=es}}</ref> By 1988, Atlantis had formed a regular [[tag team]] with [[Ángel Azteca]], defeating ''[[Los Infernales]]'' ([[Masakre]] and [[MS-1 (wrestler)|MS-1]]) to win the [[Mexican National Tag Team Championship]] on March 6.<ref name="MexTag" /> Three months later, he became a double champion, defeating [[Kung Fu (wrestler)|Kung Fu]] for the [[NWA World Middleweight Championship]], the highest championship in the [[Lucha Libre#Weight classes|middleweight division]]; he lost it to [[Emilio Charles Jr.]] 37 days later.<ref name="NWAMiddle" /> He regained the title on July 20, losing it back to Charles two weeks later.<ref name="NWAMiddle" /> On May 25, 1990, after 811 days, Atlantis and Azteca lost their championship to [[Bestia Salvaje]] and [[Pierroth Jr.]],<ref name="MexTag" /> leading to a [[Narrative thread|storyline]] where Azteca attacked Atlantis, [[Glossary of professional wrestling terms#turn|turning]] ''rudo'' ([[Heel (professional wrestling)|heel]]). The feud between the two continued off and on over the years until Azteca's death in 2007; they remained close friends backstage.<ref name="MundoHispano">{{cite web|url=http://www.munhispano.com/?nid=247&sid=1008433|title=Reportan súbita muerte del luchador Angel Azteca en Campeche|date=March 19, 2007|access-date= August 11, 2009|publisher= Mundo Hispano de KSL|language=es}}</ref>

Atlantis was one of the key figures in the "rebranding" of EMLL to Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre (CMLL) in 1990. In 1991, Atlantis starred in the movie ''La Fuerza Bruta'' ("The Brute Power") and subsequently featured in another with [[Octagón]], ''Octagón y Atlantis, la revancha'' ("Octagón and Atlantis, the revenge"), which premiered in 1992. On April 4, 1991, Atlantis, Octagón, and [[Máscara Sagrada]], nicknamed "Los Movie Stars", defeated ''Los Thundercats'' (Leono, Panthro and Tigro) to win the [[Mexican National Trios Championship]], but lost it to ''[[Los Capos|Los Hermanos Dinamita]]'' ([[Cien Caras]], [[Máscara Año 2000]] and [[Universo 2000]]) on August 11.<ref name="MexTrio" /> Not long after, Octagón and Sagrada left CMLL to join the recently formed [[Lucha Libre AAA Worldwide|Asistencia Asesoría y Administración]] (AAA) before the "Atlantis y Octagón" movie premiered in theaters. Atlantis was also offered an AAA contract, but chose to stay with CMLL.<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" /> On March 3, 1993, Atlantis lost the NWA World Middleweight Championship to [[Mano Negra (wrestler)|Mano Negra]], later unmasking Negra by defeating him in a ''[[Lucha libre#Luchas de Apuestas|Lucha de Apuestas]]'' ("bet match") in the main event of the [[CMLL 60th Anniversary Show]] on October 1.<ref name="Ovaciones20999" /> On March 2, 1994, Atlantis moved to the [[Lucha Libre#Weight classes|light heavyweight division]], defeating [[Dr. Wagner Jr.]] to win the [[CMLL World Light Heavyweight Championship]], which he held for 655 days.<ref name="CMLLLHeavy" /> 

On November 3, 1995, Atlantis and [[Rayo de Jalisco Jr.]] won the [[CMLL World Tag Team Championship]] from [[Headhunters (professional wrestling)|The Headhunters]].<ref name="CMLLTag1and2" /> Despite losing the title in August 1996, Atlantis and [[Lizmark]] won it from ''La Ola Blanca'' ([[Arturo Beristain|El Hijo del Gladiador]] and [[Gran Markus Jr.]]), which was vacated twelve days later after an inconclusive match with the Headhunters.<ref name="CMLLTag1and2" /> In 1997, they and [[Mr. Niebla]] formed ''La Ola Azul'' ("The Blue Wave"), defeating Charles, [[El Satánico]] and [[Rey Bucanero]] for the [[CMLL World Trios Championship]] on April 29, holding it until an injury to Mr. Niebla forced them to give up the title in October 1998.<ref name="CMLLTrios1" /> On May 10, 1999, Atlantis defeated Wagner for his second CMLL World Light Heavyweight Championship, losing it to [[Villano III]], whom he had a long-running feud with, on November 22.<ref name="CMLLLHeavy" /> The feud culminated in a ''Lucha de Apuestas'' at ''[[Juicio Final (2000)|Juicio Final]]'' ("Final Judgment") on March 17, 2000, where Atlantis unmasked Villano III in a match that was voted the ''[[Wrestling Observer Newsletter]]''<nowiki/>'s 2000 [[Wrestling Observer Newsletter awards#Match of the Year|Match of the Year]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Luchas 2000|work=Atlantis y sus Victimas|publisher=Publicaciones citem, S.A. de C.V.|location=[[Ciudad Juárez|Juárez]], [[Mexico]]|id=Especial 30|pages=32–36|language=es}}</ref> On June 16, 2002, Atlantis, Mr. Niebla and [[Black Warrior (wrestler)|Black Warrior]] defeated [[Blue Panther]], [[Fuerza Guerrera]] and Wagner to win the trios championship, holding it for 278 days.<ref name="CMLLTrios2" /> On June 25, 2004, Atlantis and Blue Panther defeated ''[[Los Guerreros del Infierno]]'' ([[Último Guerrero]] and Bucanero) to win the CMLL World Tag Team Championship. By this time, Atlantis was stagnating as a ''tecnico'', prompting him to turn on Panther during a title match, ending their reign at 280 days and turning ''rudo'' for the first time in his career.<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" />

==== ''Los Guerreros de la Atlantida'' (2005–2011) ====
{{main|Los Guerreros del Infierno}}
The ''rudo'' Atlantis subsequently joined ''Los Guerreros del Infierno'', which was renamed ''Los Guerreros de la Atlantida'' ("The Warriors of the Atlantis") out of respect for their new co-leader.<ref name=FigurasAtlantis/> 2005 turned out to be Atlantis' strongest and most successful year, as he won the [[CMLL International Gran Prix#International Gran Prix 2005|International Gran Prix]] ,<ref name=PWHGP2005/> the [[NWA World Light Heavyweight Championship]],<ref name="CMLLTrios3" /> and that year's ''[[Leyenda de Plata#Leyenda de Plata 2005|Leyenda de Plata]]'' ("The Silver Legend") tournament.<ref name="Plata2005" /> On September 29, 2009, ''Los Guerrero de la Atlantida'' won the vacant CMLL World Trios Championship by defeating Aguayo Jr., [[Héctor Garza]] and [[Shocker (wrestler)|Shocker]] in a tournament final.<ref name="CMLLTrios3" /> On November 2, Atlantis won his fourth CMLL World Tag Team Championship, this time teaming with Último Guerrero to defeat [[Místico]] and [[Negro Casas]].<ref name=CMLLTag3/>

[[File:LuchadorAtlantis.jpg|thumb|Atlantis often wore a red mask as a ''rudo''|195x195px]]
On January 22, 2010, Atlantis and [[Gran Metalik|Máscara Dorada]] participated in the ''[[CMLL Torneo Nacional de Parejas Increíbles (2010)|Torneo Nacional de Parejas Increibles]]'' ("National Incredible Pairs Tournament"), where a ''tecnico'' is paired with a ''rudo''. They defeated [[Dragón Rojo Jr.]] and [[Andrade El Idolo|La Sombra]] in the first round, Mr. Niebla and [[Máximo (wrestler)|Máximo]] in the quarter-finals and Místico and [[Averno (wrestler)|Averno]] in the semi-finals.<ref name=Jan22>{{cite web|url=http://Superluchas.com/2010/01/23/cmll-en-la-arena-mexico-viernes-22-de-enero-2010-mistico-se-vuelve-rudo/|title=MLL en la Arena México (Viernes 22 de enero 2010) – ¿Místico se vuelve rudo?|author=Velazquez, Israel|date=January 23, 2010|access-date=January 28, 2010|work=[[Súper Luchas]]|language=es}}</ref> On February 5, Atlantis (wrestling as a ''tecnico'' and donning his old white mask) and Dorada defeated Casas and La Máscara in the finals to win the tournament.<ref name=CMLLFeb5>{{cite web|url=http://Superluchas.com/2010/02/06/resultados-arena-mexico-5-feb-10-ahora-si-mistico-super-rudo/|title=Resultados Arena México 5 February 10 – áhora si Místico Súper Rudo! – Atlantis y Máscara Dorada ganadores de tornero de parejas Increibles|author=Ocampo, Ernesto|date=February 6, 2010|access-date=February 7, 2010|work=[[Súper Luchas]]|language=es}}</ref> On July 12, at the [[Promociones Gutiérrez 1st Anniversary Show]], Atlantis participated in a match where ten men from five ''[[Professional wrestling tag team match types#Parejas Suicidas|parejas increibles]]'' teams put their mask on the line, with the losing team being forced to wrestle each other for their masks. [[Olímpico]] was his partner, facing off against the teams of Místico and [[El Oriental]], La Sombra and [[Histeria (wrestler)|Histeria]], [[El Alebrije]] and [[Volador Jr.]], and Averno and Guerrero.<ref name=10Masks>{{cite web|url=http://Superluchas.com/2010/06/26/el-12-de-julio-caera-una-mascara-en-nuevo-laredo-en-la-funcion-de-aniversario-de-promociones-gutierrez/|title=El 12 de julio caerá una máscara en Nuevo Laredo en la función de aniversario de Promociones Gutierrez|author=Flores, Manuel|date=June 26, 2010|access-date=July 1, 2010|work=[[Súper Luchas]]|language=es}}</ref> They were ultimately the last team to escape the match.<ref name=Ruleta2010>{{cite web|url=http://Superluchas.com/2010/07/13/oriental-pierde-la-mascara-ante-mistico-en-nuevo-laredo/|title=El Oriental pierde la máscara ante Místico en Nuevo Laredo|date=July 13, 2010|access-date=July 13, 2010|work=[[Súper Luchas]]|language=es}}</ref> At the [[CMLL 77th Anniversary Show]] on September 3, Atlantis was one of fourteen men putting their mask on the line in a steel cage ''Lucha de Apuestas'', keeping it safe as the ninth man to leave the cage.<ref name=Aniversario77Live>{{cite web|url=http://Superluchas.com/2010/09/03/cobertura-cmll-el-juicio-final-lxxvii-aniversario-de-la-empresa-mexicana-de-lucha-libre/|title=Cobertura CMLL: El Juicio Final. LXXVII Aniversario de la Empresa Mexicana de Lucha Libre|author=Ocampo, Jorge|date=September 3, 2010|access-date=September 4, 2010|work=[[Súper Luchas]]|language=es}}</ref>

'''Gilbert Vincent Perkins''' (24 August 1907 – 28 March 1999) was an Australian film and television actor.

==Early life==

As a teenager, Perkins was a trackman and an athlete.  He ran away from home at a young age and joined the crew of a [[Norway|Norwegian]] cargo ship as a deck hand.

==Early career==

In his early adult life, he left for [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]].  He modified his Australian accent to be more British-sounding so that he could portray British characters.  His first role was as an extra for ''[[The Divine Lady]]'' in 1929, while his first credited role was as Sgt. Cox in ''[[Journey's End]]'' the following year.

==Career peak==

Eventually, Perkins became a regular stuntman for [[William Boyd (actor)|William Boyd]].  He also did stunt work for [[Bruce Cabot]] in ''[[King Kong (1933 film)|King Kong]]'' and [[Spencer Tracy]] in ''[[Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1941 film)|Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde]]''.  He also worked for Universal Pictures in ''[[Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man]]''.  Throughout his career, he acted and did stunts in many feature films and television shows.  In 1956 Perkins appeared as Mingo in the TV western ''[[Cheyenne (TV series)|Cheyenne]]'' in the episode titled "Johnny Bravo."

He also did some [[special effect]] work, normally for action sequences. He appeared as a Gladiator in ''[[Demetrius and the Gladiators]]'', a sequel to [[20th Century Fox]]'s biblical epic, ''[[The Robe (film)|The Robe]]''. He was already 50 years of age when he played the "teenaged" monster in the [[1958 in film|1958]] [[science fiction film|science fiction]]/[[horror film]] ''[[Teenage Monster]]''.<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0051063/ IMDb, ''Teenage Monster'', 1958.]</ref>

==Later works and death==

In 1960, Gil Perkins co-founded the [[Stuntmen's Association of Motion Pictures]].  Four years later, he became the treasurer of the [[Screen Actors Guild]], a position he held for fifteen years.  His official retirement was in 1972, though he continued working for some years later.  His last acting role was in ''[[Raging Bull]]'' in 1980, but his last credited role was as a fantasy lover in ''Odyssey, the Ultimate Trip''.  He died in [[Woodland Hills, Los Angeles|Woodland Hills]], Los Angeles, of natural causes, and was [[cremated]] with his ashes scattered at sea.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FOHgDAAAQBAJ&dq=gil+perkins+cremated+ashes+scattered+at+sea&pg=PA584 | title=Resting Places: The Burial Sites of More Than 14,000 Famous Persons, 3d ed | isbn=9781476625997 | last1=Wilson | first1=Scott | date=19 August 2016 | publisher=McFarland }}</ref>

'''Richard Curwen Wordsworth''' (19 January 1915 – 21 November 1993) was an English [[character actor]].<ref name=":0">[https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-richard-wordsworth-1507468.html ''Independent'' obituary 29 Nov 1993]</ref> He was the great-great-grandson of the poet [[William Wordsworth]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Theater Professor Had Poetic Roots |url=https://magazine.utdallas.edu/2018/11/05/theater-professor-had-poetic-roots/ |access-date=2025-08-13 |website=UT Dallas Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and career==
As a young man he followed in the footsteps of his clergyman father, reading Divinity at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]]. But he quickly found acting more to his taste and, after performing at the [[Footlights|Cambridge Footlights]], he decided to study drama at the [[Embassy Theatre (London)|Embassy School of Acting]] in London.

This proved an excellent choice. He quickly developed a talent for character acting which sustained him and his family through a long and richly varied career. In classical theatre he worked with [[John Gielgud]], [[Donald Wolfit]], [[Anthony Quayle]]<ref name=":0" /> and [[Richard Burton]]. After successful Shakespearian seasons at [[the Old Vic]] and [[Stratford-upon-Avon]], he starred in the musical ''[[Lock Up Your Daughters (musical)|Lock Up Your Daughters]]'' which launched the [[Mermaid Theatre]] in London. He also found success as Captain Hook in several Christmas productions of ''Peter Pan''. Later he would tour Australia as Fagin in the musical ''Oliver'' which he also produced.

His film career included a standout performance as the monstrous astronaut in ''[[The Quatermass Xperiment]]'', which launched [[Hammer Film Productions]]’ famous run as the UK’s foremost producers of horror movies. Later he played a scene as a sinister taxidermist with [[James Stewart]] (whom he described as 'a perfect gentleman') in [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s second version of [[The Man Who Knew Too Much (1956 film)|''The Man Who Knew Too Much'']]. He also played leading parts in British TV dramas such as ''[[Huntingtower (novel)#Adaptations|Huntingtower]]'' and ''[[The Tripods (TV series)|The Tripods]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Richard Wordsworth {{!}} Actor |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0941416/ |access-date=2025-08-26 |website=IMDb |language=en-US}}</ref>

In the final decades of his life he developed ''The Bliss of Solitude'' a one-man tribute to his great ancestor with which he toured Britain and the United States. He also founded the Wordsworth Summer School – a week of poetry, lectures and walks in his beloved [[Lake District]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Steedman |first=Carolyn |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/History_and_the_Law/ntTKDwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22Wordsworth+Summer+School%22&pg=PA34&printsec=frontcover |title=History and the Law: A Love Story |date=2020-01-30 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-48605-7 |language=en}}</ref>

{{Short description|American actor (1902–1976)}} {{see also|Corriganville Movie Ranch}} {{Use American English|date=September 2021}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2021}} {{More citations needed|date=May 2017}} {{Infobox person | name = Ray "Crash" Corrigan | image = Ray Corrigan The White Gorilla.jpg | caption = Corrigan in ''[[The White Gorilla]]'' (1945) | birth_name = Raymond Benitz | birth_date = {{Birth date|1902|02|14|mf=yes}} | birth_place = [[Milwaukee, Wisconsin]], U.S. | death_date = {{Death date and age|1976|08|10|1902|02|14|mf=yes}} | death_place = [[Brookings, Oregon]], U.S. | resting_place = [[Inglewood Park Cemetery]], California | other_names = Raymond Benard
Ray Benard
Gorilla | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1932–1958 | spouse = {{plainlist| * {{marriage|Rita Jane Smeal|1920|1954|end=divorced}} * {{marriage|Elaine DuPont|1956|1967|end=divorced}} }} | children = 3 }} '''Ray''' "'''Crash'''" '''Corrigan''' (born '''Raymond Benitz'''; February 14, 1902 – August 10, 1976) was an American actor most famous for appearing in many [[B-movie|B-Western]] movies (among these the ''[[Three Mesquiteers]]'' and ''[[Range Busters|The Range Busters]]'' film series). He also was a [[stuntman]] and frequently acted as [[silver screen]] gorillas using his own [[Gorilla suit|gorilla costume]]s. In 1937, Corrigan purchased land in the [[Santa Susana Mountains]] foothills in [[Simi Valley]] and developed it into a [[movie ranch]] called "[[Corriganville Movie Ranch|Corriganville]]". The [[movie ranch]] was used for [[location filming]] in film serials, feature films, and television shows, as well as for the performance of live western shows for tourists. Bob Hope later bought the ranch in 1966 and renamed it "Hopetown". It is now a Regional Park and nature preserve.[http://www.lamountains.com/parks.asp?parkid=99 "Corriganville Park"], LAMountains.com; retrieved June 23, 2013. {{TOC limit|limit=2}} ==Film career== [[File:New Frontier (1939) 1.jpg|thumb|In ''[[New Frontier (film)|New Frontier]]'' (1939), L-R: Corrigan, [[Jennifer Jones]] and [[John Wayne]] ]] Corrigan's Hollywood career began as a [[Physical fitness|physical fitness instructor]] and [[physical culture]] trainer to the stars. In the early 1930s he did stunts and bit parts in several films, billed as '''Ray Benard'''. Many of his early roles were in ape costumes, for example, as a gorilla in ''[[Tarzan and His Mate]]'' (1934) and an "orangopoid" in the first [[Flash Gordon (serial)|''Flash Gordon'' serial]]. ===Republic Pictures=== In [[1936 in film|1936]], Corrigan had his screen breakthrough with the starring role in a [[Republic Pictures|Republic]] serial, ''[[The Undersea Kingdom]]'', which evoked memories of [[Universal Pictures|Universal]]'s first "[[Flash Gordon]]" serial. His character was known as Ray "Crash" Corrigan, and he adopted it as his screen name. He followed playing the role of [[John C. Fremont]] in the Western serial ''[[The Vigilantes Are Coming]]''. On the basis of this, Republic signed him to their standard Term Player Contract, running from May 25, 1936, to May 24, 1938. He was cast as one of the trio in the ''[[Three Mesquiteers]]'' series of westerns, starring in 24 of the 51 "3M" films made by the studio. He later left Republic in 1938 over a pay dispute. Over at [[Monogram Pictures]], Corrigan began a new series of feature westerns shot at Corriganville, ''[[Range Busters|The Range Busters]]'', cheap knock-offs of The Three Mesquiteers, with a series character that used his name; between 1940 and 1943, he starred in 20 of the 24 films in this series. ===Gorilla Man=== Following this, his on-screen work largely returned to appearing in ape costumes, beginning with ''[[Three Missing Links]]'' (1938), followed by roles in ''[[The Strange Case of Doctor Rx]]'' (1942), ''[[Captive Wild Woman]]'' (1943), ''[[Nabonga]]'' (1944), ''[[White Pongo]]'' (1945) and as a prehistoric sloth in ''[[Unknown Island]]'' (1948). The original gorilla "mask" seen in films like ''[[The Ape (1940 film)|The Ape]]'' (1940) was replaced with a subtler design with a more mobile jaw. Corrigan sold his gorilla suits in 1948 and provided training in using them to their new owner, [[Steve Calvert]], a [[Ciro's]] bartender. Calvert stepped into Corrigan's paw prints starting with a [[Jungle Jim]] film starring [[Johnny Weissmuller]]. Despite reports to the contrary, Calvert and Corrigan never appeared together on-screen in an ape costume. Since both Corrigan and Calvert eschewed screen credit playing gorillas, their film credits are often confused; any appearance of the "Corrigan suit" after 1948 is by Calvert. His final theatrical film was playing the title role in the [[science fiction film]] ''[[It! The Terror from Beyond Space]]'', according to bio information given to visitors at the Thousand Oaks, California, ''Corrigan's Steak House and Bar'' that his son Tom once owned. ===Television series=== In 1950, he had a television show called ''Crash Corrigan's Ranch''.{{cite book |last1=Woolery |first1=George W. |title=Children's Television: The First Thirty-Five Years, 1946-1981, Part II: Live, Film, and Tape Series |date=1985 |publisher=The Scarecrow Press |isbn=0-8108-1651-2 |pages=131–133}} He also planned a television series called ''Buckskin Rangers'' with his old associate [[Max Terhune]].[http://www.jjonz.us/RadioLogs/pagesnfiles/logs_files_RH/1950s_RH/50-54/1950/50rh_10Oct/50-10-08-(Sun)_%5BLBP%5D.pdf "New Series of Westerns Planned for Television."] ''Long Beach Press-Telegram'', October 8, 1950. ==Corriganville== In 1937, Corrigan was on a hunting trip with [[Clark Gable]] when he had an idea to purchase land in [[Simi Valley]], [[California]], and use it as a Western-themed ranch similar to [[Iverson Movie Ranch]]. He paid a $1,000 down payment, then a thousand dollars a month until the $11,354 price was paid.Gilpatrick [https://books.google.com/books?id=kKPcSwYtbQUC&pg=PA202 2002, p. 202.] He developed this into [[Corriganville Movie Ranch|Corriganville]], a location used for many [[Western (genre)|Western]] films and TV shows. The location featured many different types of terrain for producers such as lakes, mountains, and caves.Corrigan, Ray. [http://www.phantomranch.net/bwestern/corrigan.htm "An Introduction to Corriganville."] ''The Corriganville Gazette'', Volume 1, Issue 3. Not merely set fronts, Corriganville contained actual buildings where film crews could live{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2sKkFbaVkRIC&pg=PA21|title=Corriganville Movie Ranch|first=Jerry L.|last=Schneider|date=1 August 2007|publisher=Lulu Press, Incorporated|isbn=9781430312246 |access-date=1 May 2017|via=Google Books}} and store their equipment to save the time and expense of daily travel from studios to an outdoor location. Corrigan profited well from renting this location to film studios and from paying visitors. In 1949, Corrigan opened his ranch to the public on weekends for Western-themed entertainment. The weekend attractions included stuntmen shows throughout the day, a Cavalry fort set, an outlaw shack, a full western town with saloon, jail, and hotel, live western music, Indian crafts, stagecoach rides, pony rides, and boating on the ranch's artificial lake. It was common for film and TV personalities to appear in person for photos and autographs, attracting as many as 20,000 people on weekends. Examples of [[feature film]]s and TV shows that were filmed at Corriganville: *''[[Drums of Fu Manchu]]'' (1939) *''[[Fort Apache (film)|Fort Apache]]'' (1948) *''[[The Lone Ranger (TV series)|The Lone Ranger]]'' (1949–1957) *''[[The Cisco Kid (TV series)|The Cisco Kid]]'' (1950–1956) *''[[The Adventures of Kit Carson]]'' (1951–1955) *''[[The Adventures of Rin Tin Tin]]'' (1954–1959) *''[[Have Gun – Will Travel]]'' (1957–1963) *''[[Casey Jones (TV series)|Casey Jones]]'' (1957) Hollywood cowboy stars who filmed there include: [[Gene Autry]], [[Roy Rogers]], [[Buster Crabbe]], [[John Wayne]], [[Smiley Burnette]], [[Clayton Moore]], [[Jay Silverheels]], [[Charles Starrett]], [[Ken Maynard]], [[Hoot Gibson]], [[Bob Steele (actor)|Bob Steele]], [[Tex Ritter]], and Corrigan himself. Corriganville was eventually sold to [[Bob Hope]] in 1966, becoming ''Hopetown''. Today, what remains is known as Corriganville Park and features some of the old landmarks. Signs along a hiking trail point out the historic features. ==Nickname== The origin of the "Crash" nickname is from his football-playing days. This was verified by Corrigan himself when he was a contestant on the June 11, 1959, episode of ''[[You Bet Your Life]]'' starring [[Groucho Marx]]. When asked how he got the name "Crash", Corrigan told Groucho, "When I would go to tackle somebody or instead of fighting them with my fists, I would just take off and dive at them head first and that's how I acquired the name 'Crash'". His first starring role using the name professionally was in the [[Republic Pictures]]' serial ''[[The Undersea Kingdom]]'' (1936), in which his screen character was also named "Crash Corrigan". The serial was created to capitalize on the popularity of [[Universal Pictures]]' ''[[Flash Gordon]]'' serials, and the nickname may have been appropriated by Republic's publicity department to create a similarly named hero.Anderson, Chuck. [https://web.archive.org/web/20091001213701/http://www.b-westerns.com/crash.htm "Ray 'Crash' Corrigan."] ''B-Westerns'', October 1, 2009. ==Death== Following his death from a heart attack at age 74 on August 10, 1976, in Brookings Harbor, Oregon, Ray "Crash" Corrigan was interred at [[Inglewood Park Cemetery]], [[Inglewood, California]]. '''John Alexander''' (November 29, 1897 – July 13, 1982) was an American stage, film, and television actor.

==Early life==
He was born on November 29, 1897, in [[Newport, Kentucky]]. His father owned steamboats and his mother was a [[telegraph operator]].{{cn|date=August 2022}}

==Career==
He had a career spanning more than 55 years on Broadway with his first role as the title character in ''Elmer Brown, the Only Boy in Town'' in 1908/1909.<ref name=NewYorkT>{{cite news| newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/15/obituaries/john-alexander-85-film-and-stage-actor.html| title=John Alexander, 85; Film and Stage Actor| date=July 15, 1982| url-access=subscription}}</ref>

He is best remembered for his performance as Teddy Brewster, a lunatic who thinks he is [[Theodore Roosevelt]], in the 1944 classic film ''[[Arsenic and Old Lace (film)|Arsenic and Old Lace]]'' opposite [[Cary Grant]]. He had previously portrayed that role in the 1941 [[Broadway theater|Broadway]] [[Arsenic and Old Lace (play)|play of the same name]] on which the film was based. He went on to play the "real" Roosevelt in the 1950 [[Bob Hope]] comedy ''[[Fancy Pants (film)|Fancy Pants]]'' and reprised his role as Teddy "Roosevelt" Brewster in the 1955 TV adaptation of ''Arsenic and Old Lace'' in the anthology series ''[[The Best of Broadway]]''.

Among his other notable film roles, Alexander played Steve Edwards in ''[[A Tree Grows in Brooklyn (1945 film)|A Tree Grows in Brooklyn]]'' in 1945, Mr. McComber in ''[[Summer Holiday (1948 film)|Summer Holiday]]'' in 1948, Jack Riker in ''[[Winchester '73]]'' in 1950 and Howard Shipley in ''[[The Marrying Kind]]'' in 1952.

During the 1950s and early 1960, he guest starred on television series, such as ''[[The Phil Silvers Show]]'', ''[[Adventures of the Sea Hawk]]'' and ''[[Car 54, Where Are You?]]'' Alexander's last performance was as Mayor Crane in the Broadway comedy ''[[Never Too Late (play)|Never Too Late]]'', a role he had played since 1962.

Alexander died on July 13, 1982, in New York City.<ref name="NewYorkT"/> He is buried in the Actors Fund of America plot in [[Kensico Cemetery]] in [[Valhalla, New York]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wilson |first1=Scott |title=Resting Places: The Burial Sites of More Than 14,000 Famous Persons, 3d ed. |date=19 August 2016 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-1-4766-2599-7 |page=14 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FOHgDAAAQBAJ&q=Mary+Alden |access-date=January 22, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

'''George D. Barrows''' (New York, February 7, 1914 – Oxnard, October 17, 1994) was an American actor known for playing Ro-Man in the film ''[[Robot Monster]]''.<ref name=TVGuide>{{cite web|url=https://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/george-barrows/credits/3030246510/| title=George Barrows|website=TVGuide.com|publisher=[[TV Guide]]|access-date=10 December 2021}}</ref> He was the son of actor [[Henry A. Barrows]]. He often wore a [[gorilla suit]] for his film roles.<ref name=cb>{{cite news| title=Museum| url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/162010531/| newspaper=The Los Angeles Times| date=November 16, 1999| page=211| via=Newspapers.com| access-date=May 13, 2024}}</ref> Excluding his gorilla roles, Barrows usually played bit parts in films and was rarely credited for his work.

==Career==
Barrows built the gorilla suit he used in ''Robot Monster,'' ''[[Gorilla at Large]],'' and other films. It is currently in the collection of the [[Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County]].<ref name=cb />

He also appeared in the [[game show]] ''[[Who Do You Trust?|Do You Trust Your Wife?]]''.<ref name=quiz>{{cite news| title=Quizzers Raise $100 Week Take| url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/638348533/| newspaper=Fort Worth Star-Telegram| date=March 13, 1957| page=41| via=Newspapers.com| access-date=May 13, 2024}}</ref>

'''Don Megowan''' (May 24, 1922 – June 26, 1981) was an American actor. He played the [[Gill-man]] on land in ''[[The Creature Walks Among Us]]'', the final part of the ''[[Creature from the Black Lagoon]]'' [[trilogy]].

==Early life==
Don Megowan was born in [[Inglewood, California]] to Robert and Leila (née Dale) Megowan. His mother Leila worked as a [[negative cutting|negative cutter]] for [[Pathé]]. At {{height|ft=6|in=7}} Megowan was very active in sports, playing baseball, football, and throwing discus. He went to the [[University of Southern California]] on a football scholarship before serving in the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] during [[World War II]].<ref name= "Father">[http://www.classicimages.com/features/article_265d96ba-8841-11e2-81f4-0019bb2963f4.html Don Megowan "Coolest Father in the World"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150225132735/http://www.classicimages.com/features/article_265d96ba-8841-11e2-81f4-0019bb2963f4.html |date=February 25, 2015 }} Interview with Vikki Megowan by Tom Weaver at [http://www.classicimages.com Classic Images.com] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191025214323/https://www.classicimages.com/ |date=October 25, 2019 }}</ref>

==Career==
Megowan starred in the [[science fiction]] films ''[[The Werewolf (1956 film)|The Werewolf]]'' in the role of Sheriff Jack Haines,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bogue |first=Mike |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1yAvDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Don+Megowan%22+%22The+Werewolf%22&pg=PA28 |title=Apocalypse Then: American and Japanese Atomic Cinema, 1951-1967 |date=2017-08-11 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-1-4766-2900-1 |pages=28 |language=en}}</ref> in ''[[The Creation of the Humanoids]]'' (1962) as a [[Captain (OF-2)|captain]] in the anti-robot Order of Flesh and Blood, who must stop the Humanoids,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rickman |first=Gregg |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4WvwdBhKMeAC&dq=%22Don+Megowan%22+%22The+Creation+of+the+Humanoids%22&pg=PA154 |title=The Science Fiction Film Reader |date=2004 |publisher=Hal Leonard Corporation |isbn=978-0-87910-994-3 |pages=154 |language=en}}</ref> and in ''The Creature Walks Among Us'' as the [[Gill-man]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Weaver |first=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L8PK4jszVDoC&dq=%22Don+Megowan%22+%22The+Creature+Walks+Among+Us%22&pg=RA1-PA327 |title=Return of the B Science Fiction and Horror Heroes: The Mutant Melding of Two Volumes of Classic Interviews |date=2000 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-0-7864-0755-2 |pages=327 |language=en}}</ref>

Megowan also appeared in [[Western film|Westerns]]: ''[[Davy Crockett, King of the Wild Frontier]]'' (1955), ''[[The Great Locomotive Chase]]'' (1956), ''[[Snowfire]]'' (1958), ''[[Tarzan and the Valley of Gold]]'' (1966), ''[[The Devil's Brigade (film)|The Devil's Brigade]]'' (1968), and [[Mel Brooks]] ''[[Blazing Saddles]]'' (1974), in which he is credited as "Gum Chewer," but actually played the cowboy who walked up on stage to [[Madeline Kahn]] during her saloon number.

In 1962, he starred with [[Cameron Mitchell (actor)|Cameron Mitchell]] in the [[television series]], ''[[The Beachcomber (TV series)|The Beachcomber]]''. He guest starred in various programs, including the Westerns: ''[[Gunsmoke]]'' (twice), ''[[Wagon Train]]'' (twice), ''[[The Californians (TV series)|The Californians]]'', ''[[The Tall Man (TV series)|The Tall Man]]'', ''[[Maverick (TV series)|Maverick]]'', ''[[Cimarron City (TV series)|Cimarron City]]'', ''[[Have Gun–Will Travel]]'', ''[[Tales of Wells Fargo]]'', ''[[The Rifleman]]'', ''[[Lawman (TV series)|Lawman]]'', ''[[Cheyenne (1955 TV series)|Cheyenne]]'', ''[[Colt .45 (TV series)|Colt .45]]'', ''[[Bonanza]]'', ''[[The Americans (1961 TV series)|The Americans]]'', ''[[Rawhide (TV series)|Rawhide]]'', and ''[[Daniel Boone (1964 TV series)|Daniel Boone]]''. He was also cast in episodes of such series as ''[[Angel (1960 TV series)|Angel]]'', U.S. Marshal, ''[[Get Smart]]'', and ''[[Fantasy Island (1977 TV series)|Fantasy Island]]''.

==Death==
Megowan, a smoker from age 12 to 48, died of throat cancer at age 59. His weight had dwindled from nearly 300 pounds to barely 150.<ref name= "Father"/> He is interred in [[Inglewood Park Cemetery]] in [[Inglewood, California]].<ref>Wilson, Scott. ''Resting Places: The Burial Sites of More Than 14,000 Famous Persons'', 3d ed.: 2 (Kindle Locations 25047-25048). McFarland & Company, Inc., Publishers. Kindle Edition.</ref>

'''Anthony Asbury''' is an American actor and puppeteer. He has been working as a puppeteer for over three decades.

==Career==
Asbury, a native of [[Arlington, Texas]], began his career as a puppeteer on the [[ITV Network|ITV]] satire show ''[[Spitting Image]]'', where he performed a majority of characters between 1984 and 1992, these included voicing several of the characters including [[Pope John Paul II]], [[John McEnroe]], and [[Edwin Meese]], together with [[Steve Nallon]] he was the puppeteer for [[Margaret Thatcher]] from the second season. It was on Spitting Image that he met [[Louise Gold]], who introduced Asbury to [[Jim Henson]], who at the time was currently in the proceeds of production for ''[[Labyrinth (1986 film)|Labyrinth]]''. Henson invited Asbury to perform some of the creatures for the film, he was the puppeteer for Firey 5, One of the Four Guards, Right Door Knocker. He later remained associated with the Henson company, performing puppets for other film and television roles these included ''[[The Witches (1990 film)|The Witches]]'', ''[[The Flintstones (film)|The Flintstones]]'', and ''[[The Wubbulous World of Dr. Seuss]]''.

Asbury's other roles include ''[[Little Shop of Horrors (film)|Little Shop of Horrors]]'' and ''[[Absolutely Fabulous]]''.
